subtopic: RELIGIOUS INTOLERANCE IN POLAND
RELIGIOUS INTOLERANCE IN POLAND
speechtext: Has the Secretary of State for External Affairs checked the accuracy of the report on religious intolerance in Poland where over two million children are affected or involved, as contained in the Globe and Mail, June 15, page three and, if so, what steps does the government intend to take in this matter?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RELIGIOUS INTOLERANCE IN POLAND
speechtext:
In connection with the question asked by the member for St. John's East, I would like to inform the house that I have asked our embassy in Warsaw to check the accuracy of this report of religious intolerance in Poland. I have now been advised by our embassy in Warsaw that the Globe and Mail article was substantially accurate. The problem raised by the Globe and Mail article apparently dates back to a law passed by the Polish parliament in the summer of 1961 forbidding religious education in schools. This law was interpreted by the Polish authorities as applying to summer camps as well, and priests have consequently been barred from conducting services within them.
As the house is aware, the Canadian government is against any form of religious intolerance. However, it is felt that any action taken by the government in this regard might have an effect contrary to that intended and could be interpreted as an intrusion in the internal affairs of another country. Considering these possible repercussions, the government does not propose to take action at the present time, beyond the informal inquiries we have made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: LETTER RESPECTING GEORGIAN BAY WATER LEVEL
speechtext: The Prime Minister received a letter dated April 28 from the Georgian bay development association containing certain suggestions about the improvement of the water levels in the lake Huron basin. Action taken by the government concerning the water levels in lake Huron and Georgian bay has included an emergency dredging program, already announced in the house by the Minister of Public Works, and a request to the governments of Ontario and Quebec for their concurrence in a proposed reference to the international joint commission for a study of methods of regulating the whole great lakes-St. Lawrence basin, since the present regulatory regime under the international joint commission is confined to lake Superior, lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence river. In order to bring about some improvement in water levels in the St. Mary's river and lake Huron, the international joint commission recently authorized an increase in the outflow from lake Superior of 10,000 cubic feet per second in addition to the outflow called for by the rule curve.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
As this question concerns two departments it should be directed to the Prime Minister. It is in connection with the Cyprus situation and the apparent deterioration there in the relationship between the Cypriots and the United Nations force and the contemplated or threatened withdrawal by the contingents of Sweden and Denmark.
Is the Prime Minister in a position to say anything more than has appeared in the press in connection with this, and what is the present position in so far as the Canadian contribution is concerned?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the position, as the right hon. gentleman has stated, is most difficult and delicate. I am going to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to answer the question based on the latest telegrams which have come in this morning and which he has had more of an opportunity to examine than I have as yet.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman will understand that one would have anticipated this question, which is a proper question in the circumstances.
I would like to say in answer that the movement of troops and war material into Cyprus is of course a cause for legitimate concern. The concern of the Canadian government has been made crystal clear to the United Nations and to the countries directly concerned. Sweden and Denmark have now done likewise.
In my statement to the house on Friday I indicated the action which we had taken, in concert with certain other governments,
Inquiries of the Ministry to bring appropriate pressure to bear so that the arms build-up would be brought to a halt. In taking these actions we felt we were acting consistently as a member of the United Nations peace force in the performance of a task which at the beginning we all recognized in this house would not be an easy one. However, we did not anticipate at that time that the task would be made infinitely more difficult by clandestine action to build up the war potential on the island.
This is a matter of collective interest to all the contributing countries, and we are therefore taking collective action to obtain strict observance of the terms of the security council resolutions. Our permanent representative at the United Nations is today seeing the representatives of other contributors to the peace force, and at Canada's suggestion the group will be meeting tomorrow with senior United Nations officials concerned with the Cyprus operation. The object of what we and other contributors have been doing is to induce those directly concerned to refrain from exacerbating an already dangerous situation.
I said on Friday that the secretary general of the United Nations had made an appeal to Greece and Turkey and to the Cypriot communities. By that time there had developed a common appraisal of the extent of the arms build-up. The prime minister of Greece, Mr. Papandreou, has now replied to the United Nations secretary general and his ambassador gave me that reply this morning. I give part of it to the house. The reply, in part, reads:
I fully agree-
This is in answer to the secretary general:
' that the arms build-up in Cyprus must be halted. I am accordingly issuing a statement in which I call upon all concerned to rely upon the efforts of the United Nations peace force and the mediator for a final and lasting solution to the problems confronting Cyprus and I declare that I am looking forward to the full implementation of your program.
I may say to the right hon. gentleman that this morning I saw the Greek ambassador and the Turkish ambassador as well.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Certainly the announcement made by the prime minister of Greece is one which will be accepted with appreciation. I am sure, by all who desire to bring about an early ending of tensions and difficulties on this island. The Secretary of State for External Affairs says that strict observance of the terms under which the United Nations forces went into the island is being imposed in order to prevent an increase in the numbers of forces clandestinely infiltrating the island.

Inquiries of the Ministry Is the minister in a position to say what are the nature of the sanctions, if that is the proper expression, to ensure this strict observance; because certainly the experience of the last few weeks in what has taken place in Cyprus would not, without further elucidation, lead us to have great hopes for the future.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would hope there would be agreement on the part of other countries concerned with the suggestion which has been made regarding stabilizing the situation, establishing a freeze on the importation of men and material and adopting certain other courses which have been proposed. As to whether these will succeed I cannot say, of course, but my right hon. friend may be assured that these courses are being carefully studied and discussed in the appropriate places.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: If I may ask one other supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, it would be this. Has Canada joined with Sweden and Denmark and expressed a view similar to those views which have been expressed by the other two countries, namely that unless there is favourable action in this regard the Canadian forces would be in an impossible position under the perilous circumstances surrounding their operations?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a close examination of what was said by the foreign minister for Denmark in the statement he issued on Saturday, and of the communication addressed to the secretary general on Friday by the foreign minister for Sweden, will reveal that there was no decision to withdraw. What was involved in those communications was the suggestion, in the one case, that a security council meeting be held, and depending on the outcome, the government of Sweden would then give consideration to its future participation.
I may say to my right hon. friend that some six weeks ago I indicated in no uncertain terms that the force must be given an opportunity to carry out its obligations and that, if it was clear that this could not be done, the United Nations would have to give consideration to the position of the force. However, I do not want to say anything which would suggest that in the face of great difficulties the United Nations, called upon to deal with a difficult situation, is not prepared to meet that situation. The very suggestion of withdrawal could open up speculation which I do not believe would be justified. Suffice it to say, having in mind contingency

plans, United Nations is taking every step to discharge its responsibility under the most difficult circumstances.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: But matters have worsened so much in six weeks.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Since an announcement was made over the week end by the minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan regarding assistance to the drought stricken areas of that province, and the house has not been informed of this agreement between the federal and provincial governments, will the minister inform the house now whether this

program will be similar to the one we implemented in 1961 and which was appreciated by the farmers of that area? Will the program include a freight assistance program for the movement of fodder to these drought stricken areas of Saskatchewan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN-STEPS TO MEET CRITICAL LIVESTOCK SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was in Saskatchewan recently I arranged for P.F.R.A. to proceed immediately with an extension to the Meeting Lake community pasture which, along with some vacant capacity in the Spiritwood pasture, would enable P.F.R.A. to accommodate another 2,500 head of cattle. This was advertised widely throughout the area, both through the agricultural representatives and the press, but to date only about 100 additional head have been brought to the pastures.
This may indicate that in spite of the extremely dry weather the problem is probably more one of winter fodder than of immediate pasture or feed. There is no sign of any extensive liquidation of cattle. There are probably a few extra yearling heifers coming to market for which there is a ready outlet.
There have been some recent local showers in the north, particularly in the Melfort area, and where these have occurred the grass is reported to be picking up quickly.
The province of Saskatchewan is introducing a program of assisting in the transportation cost of moving fodder to the drought area, of moving haying machinery and of trucking cattle to feed. As was the case in 1961, the federal government will share the cost of this with the province on a 50-50 basis.
The community well drilling program has been extended for the fiscal year 1964-65. Under this program the municipality pays 30 per cent of the cost and the provincial and federal governments share the balance.
These are the measures which have been taken to deal with the immediate situation. We are discussing also with the province more long range measures to encourage farmers to provide fodder and water reserves against the eventuality of drought. I am not yet in a position to make a precise statement with respect to these, but I hope to do so in the not too distant future.
I should like to add that when applications are received from Quebec or Manitoba the same consideration will be given to these provinces, and to the province of Alberta, where these serious drought conditions exist.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, July 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of education and training on a large scale takes on new importance in 1964. When we think of the fact that the young people coming out of our schools need more training and education than we ever needed when we finished our schooling, we cannot but realize the significance which legislators should attribute to the education and training of the rising generation.
The fact that the cost of education is continually increasing is another reason to attach importance to this question.
Recent statistics indicate that a third of the 282,000 Canadian unemployed are young people who probably are without jobs because they are ill prepared to occupy more important positions when they enter the labour field after leaving school.
The legislation now before us, Bill No. C-110, provides for student loans. The object
Loans to Students
of this legislation is most important and even excellent in itself. Indeed, it is very laudable.
However, even if those who put forward this legislation do intend to help the students, we nevertheless should look twice at their poor intentions before taking action, because I think that this government is invading a field which is not properly its own. As a matter of fact, one does not have to listen for very long to the protests with which this legislation has met to be convinced that there are many who dislike it as there are many who, like myself, say that the federal government impinges upon activities over which it has no jurisdiction. And, to add weight to the point I	am trying	to	make, I shouldlike to draw the attention	of	the house to	an
article published in La Presse of February 26, 1964. Under the title "Encroachment by consent", Mr. Vincent Prince states:
Could it be, by any chance, that Ottawa, under the cover of co-operative federalism, is trying to impose upon us	"encroachment	by consent"?
And a little	further on:
Just remember last year's legislation to enable Ottawa to grant loans to municipalities. Think especially of the federal plan now under discussion and which, this time, deals with financial assistance to students.
In my humble opinion, this is not co-operation of a federal nature, but rather an encroachment on federalism itself.
And a little further, he draws the following conclusion:
Ottawa tells tb provinces: "Let me look after municipalities and students for you. We are encroaching upon your jurisdiction but, if you agree, that becomes co-operative federalism."
Need I add that the students themselves voiced protests also and, at this stage, I refer to the comments and objections made by the various Quebec university student associations. All those bodies have expressed their opinions and objections to the authorities concerned. I should like to point out that, among those who have protested, there is the Laval University Liberal club; last Friday, one of its members stated that the legislation under consideration in the house is an encroachment of the federal government upon a field of provincial jurisdiction.
And what did Mr. Paul Sauriol say about that same legislation?
In an article published in Le Devoir on July 15, 1964, referring to comments made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), Mr. Sauriol came to the following conclusion:
That is what is called respecting the rights of the provinces. That system remains unacceptable

Loans to Students
because the central government is taking the initiative in matters which fall exclusively under provincial jurisdiction, collecting and using taxes in that way for provincial purposes, imposing controls and the terms of its program even to the provinces which would like to be kept out of it.
Mr. Clement Brown, journalist for Mont-real-Matin, is also asking himself some questions. For instance, he wonders:
Who will decide and what will be the yardstick?
In other words, Mr. Brown wonders what will be the criteria to determine who will be entitled to a loan.
He goes on:
Will it be necessary to produce one's income tax returns both to the provincial department of education and to the banks managers who, in some provinces, will administer the loans? Incidentally, what have the managers to do with the financial structures of education and the relations between the students and the institution where they are studying?
Even some rather influential Liberal members have clearly expressed their views on that point.
I should like to put on record the statement made by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) on March 18, 1964, as reported in Le Devoir:
Why should the central government help students by granting them loans while provinces could look after that much better?
And further:
Mr. Pepin advocated a new agreement on taxation sharing, stating that the present practices are based on wartime economy.
Another one who claims, Mr. Speaker, a complete disapproval of the federal government's intrusion in a field of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
What did Mr. Lesage himself say, the day after the last federal-provincial conference? Here is what he said, as reported in the Montreal-Matin of April 3, 1964:
We definitely cannot accept that, even in good faith, the federal administration make the mistake of encroaching upon a field which undeniably falls under our own jurisdiction and which moreover, we occupy, have been occupying for more than three years already.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the Minister of Finance himself recognized indirectly that the field of education comes under provincial jurisdiction when he said, as can be seen on page 5443 of Hansard for July 14, 1964:
We recognize that the provinces are better able than the federal government to determine which students require assistance for the pursuit of their education in provincial educational institutions.

This, Mr. Speaker, clearly shows that education comes under provincial jurisdiction. I would like to refer now to the election campaign of 1960 in the province of Quebec when the present premier of that province, Hon. Jean Lesage, promised free education at every level in the province of Quebec.
If the Quebec premier promised free education it was because he was convinced that education was entirely and solely under provincial jurisdiction. I am sure that he would not have promised something which was not within his jurisdiction. I think that having studied the matter, he realized that education came completely under provincial jurisdiction.
As the minister himself admitted a few minutes ago, there is in the province of Quebec a scholarship system available to students of that province who do not have the money to complete their studies.
There are also honour loans granted by the St. Jean-Baptiste society to young people anxious to further their studies. I know what I am speaking about, because every year, I canvass the city of St. Hyacinthe and the neighbourhood, to raise funds, so that the St. Jean-Baptiste society might grant loans without interest to our young people who can give proof of their honesty and of their wish to improve their knowledge.
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house is definitely an underhanded interference on the part of centralists in a field coming under exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
I shall not make a complete analysis of this legislation from a legal point of view. My hon. friend, the hon. member for Ber-thier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) did make such a complete analysis. They stated the objections that we, from the province of Quebec, should put forward to oppose this legislation and to suggest to the proper authorities, and more particularly to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), to take the necessary steps and means to guarantee that there will not be another encroachment upon provincial autonomy.
When reference is made to provincial autonomy, that does not apply only to the province of Quebec. We must also protect the other provinces that have a direct responsibility in this field of education.
Let us, in the federal field, look after matters which concern us more particularly and which come under our jurisdiction. We have

to deal with enough matters of federal jurisdiction without continuously attempting to interfere with provincial responsibilities. Let the provinces look after their own responsibilities. Being closer to the problems, the provincial governments are in a better position to solve them to the satisfaction of the parties concerned.
Incidentally, I should like to ask the minister, in his capacity of Minister of Justice, and also as a representative from the province of Quebec, to speak up for his colleagues from the province of Quebec who surely must have made representations to him. Even if it is embarrassing to accept the suggestions of the opposition, I urge him to take all necessary steps to safeguard the autonomy, the prerogatives and the rights of the province of Quebec and of the other provinces. I also ask him to see to it that a committee of the house be set up, so that the parties concerned with this problem might have an opportunity to contribute to its solution.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that the people most interested in this matter, that is the students, do not fear to rise and object to a legislation which could be favourable to them financially. There certainly must be a very serious reason for that.
It is because these young people see in the present measure a serious threat to provincial autonomy.
The seriousness with which these young people approach the question might well be stressed, and they should be encouraged to keep on considering in this way the measures which have a great bearing on their future, and on that of their province.
If the present Liberal federal government has so much surplus income that it must enter fields of provincial autonomy, I would like to make a few suggestions to solve that problem. First of all, I would advise the Minister of Finance to withdraw from taxation fields belonging specifically to the provinces and to give them jurisdiction and the greatest possibility of acquiring, through taxation, the moneys they need.
If, after taking this action it still has too much revenue, to the point where it does not know what to do with it, then, I would ask it to abandon immediately the 11 per cent tax.
The legislation before us is certainly, as I said before, very commendable, but since it tends to diminish the influence and authority of other bodies, the provincial governments, and in my opinion, we, of the province of Quebec, should object. Besides, that is what
Loans to Students
I intend to do as soon as the legislation comes before us for consideration, and after the few remarks I still have to make.
I feel, as an obligation toward my electors of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, that I must do everything I can to protect provincial autonomy.
In 1957, when I first sought to be elected by my fellow citizens in my riding, I deplored at the time that provincial autonomy had not been respected by the Liberal government. I suggested that if provincial autonomy was not respected, if it was trodden underfoot, it was because here, in this House of Commons, the province of Quebec was not represented by members who had the provincial autonomy at heart and were ready to stand up for it.
At the time I made, in this respect, the following pledge: If the voters of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot honoured me by sending me to the House of Commons, I would seize every opportunity to stand up for the rights and prerogatives of the provinces.
I am repeating it because, by doing so, I think that I am helping not only the province of Quebec, but all the other provinces, because the latter should also have their jurisdiction protected.
Moreover, with regard to Bill No. C-110, unless some amendments answering the claims of my hon. friend from Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere and of my desk-mate, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue (Mr. Martineau), be brought to this legislation, I shall deem it my duty to vote against the legislation, in order to protect the rights and prerogatives of the provincial governments in matters of education and training.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be rather brief this afternoon, since several members have already spoken on Bill No. C-110 concerning the making of loans to students.
First, I must say that I am expressing my own point of view and that nobody else in this house is involved in this respect. I am totally against the bill now before us, not because I am against assistance to students, for the students, as we know, are in urgent need of money, whether they are technical, high school or university students, since their holidays are rather short and it is somewhat difficult for them to find work that would permit them to pay their tuition fees.
If I object to Bill No. C-110, it is simply because, once again, the central government interferes in a field where it must not come in. In 1867, when the provinces got together to set up confederation, it was clearly decided that the field of education would remain under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and that the central government would have no say in the matter.
In every province there is a system of education which meets adequately the needs of the children and the students. We fail to see why the central government should interfere in a matter where the provincial governments are doing a good job.

In the province of Quebec we have not only an educational system but also a system of scholarships, and some associations grant loans to students. We do not see why the federal government should put grit in the bearings.
I am absolutely opposed to the intrusion of the federal government in the field of education. However, I am surprised by the attitude of the premier of the province of Quebec who approves Bill No. C-110, when we know that, not a very long while ago, he stated that he would take legal action against the federal government should the latter implement Bill No. C-110.
Today we see Mr. Lesage act like a sheep as he always did when he was a member of this parliament, get coaxed by the federal government and accept without protest Bill No. C-110, which is an intrusion of the federal government into the field of education, an exclusive responsibility of the provinces.
One does not have to be a premier to understand that; the students themselves, although they need money and know that some help would be welcome, blame the federal government which intrudes into the field of education.
If we read newspaper reports we see that the students' unions at Montreal, Quebec and Sherbrooke universities ask the federal government to withdraw this bill pending a meeting between the students themselves and the government of the province of Quebec to discuss the matter.
Here is what a newspaper of Wednesday, July 15, says:
The students federal loan bill is questionable, because it is another intrusion of the Ottawa government into the field of education, and also because it is a poor substitute for free education. This program is a real compendium of the basic faults of co-operative federalism.
A formula so eloquently advocated by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis).
Moreover, I must say that for some time now the federal government has been endeavouring to centralize everything here in Ottawa by depriving the provinces of rights which confederation reserved for them, by invading more and more fields which had been made the exclusive responsibility of the provinces.
We have our school boards which are responsible for our children's education. When they are unable to do so or when they lack the necessary money, because the provincial or the federal governments collect taxes from the taxpayers, leaving nothing to the school

boards, the latter have to ask the provincial government for the necessary money to meet the needs of their respective parishes. We can thus see that the federal government tries to centralize more and more and we can understand Hon. Jean Lesage's attitude. In fact, in 1953 and 1954, he was advocating greater centralization here, in Ottawa; we are not surprised then that he lets the federal government intrude into provincial fields and infringe upon rights and prerogatives that are exclusively provincial.
As an hon. member from the province of Quebec mentioned last week, would that not be a first stage in a policy which will soon lead to the creation of a federal department of education? If we must come to that, it would be unfortunate that in 1964 hon. members would have been gulled by the student loans since, later on, they will have to answer to the federal department of education.
I do not think that the setting up of a federal department of education is the thing to do, because each province has its own mentality, its own educational system which meets its requirements and the needs of its inhabitants. If we are to pass this bill and set up in a few years a federal department of education, I believe that many of us will live to regret it.
As it is difficult enough to come to an agreement among the various provinces, more particularly when mutual understanding between the two great races in Canada enters into it, we should not widen the gap on purpose and aggravate the slight uneasiness which seems to exist between those two great Canadian races.
I am surprised that several pieces of legislation which are now submitted by the federal government apparently just seek to widen the gap between the two great races in Canada, instead of uniting them.
We have now a Liberal government, the Pearson government, which seems bent on widening this gap. It would be unfortunate that following this Bill No. C-110, and various other pieces of legislation, we should later on have to regret that the Liberal government which was to solve and unite everything in Canada, was the greatest disrupting agent of our times.
Mr. Speaker, I am against Bill No. C-110, because there is enough patronage now in the province of Quebec without any need of more patronage here in Ottawa. We have enough trouble with this scholarship and bursary situation as it is without our being
Loans to Students
subjected to this new form of patronage which is now familiar to us in Quebec.
We know that those who need money most often get the smallest scholarships and have the greatest difficulty in obtaining them. In short, when students are on the right side, that is in favour of the party in office, it is easy for them to get those scholarships, but if a student happens to be poor and his family's political allegiance is not to the government in office, that is where the trouble starts.
I see other difficulties coming up when the time comes for a student loan and a father or a son has to see the bank manager. There again, there will be some sort of muzzle, since the bank manager will surely be aware of the father's political affiliation, and that is where you will have patronage. That is where pressure will be exerted and the student's father will be made to promise that, if he wants his son to have his scholarship for the next five years, he will have to change his political colour, mind his tongue and stop discussing, or simply refer to the supposedly good legislation passed by the government in office.
Many employees of the province of Quebec have already been gagged. Just go and talk, for instance, to people working on roads for the provincial government. There you will find persons with a chain around their necks and who cannot utter a word because, should they speak against the party in power, they would simply have to go back home.
Do not be surprised at this assertion, Mr. Speaker, because as a result of a survey among the street sweepers and those engaged in road maintenance in my parish, I was not able to find a single employee who was not a sympathizer of the Liberal party or who had not been recognized as such for a number of generations.
I realize that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) is applauding, but I must tell him that the same situation existed when Mr. Duplessis was in power, just as it exists today under Mr. Lesage.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to refer again to Beauchesne's citation No. 382 which also applies in this case. It is true that, under the proposed amendment, we are going against the principle of the bill, but, according to citation No. 382, page 277 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, we can move an amendment to or a motion against Bill No. C-110 now before us.
The argument put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is that this amendment is not relevant to the principle of the bill.
The bill deals with loans to students while the amendment deals with scholarships to students. But, if we take a second look at citation No. 382, we find that it deals with assistance to students, whether under the form of loans or scholarships.
Citation No. 382 states:

It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons lor not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or different from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill-

Then we wish to make a statement of principle adverse to the principle of Bill No. C-110. We want scholarships for students, instead of student loans. We want this to be done under the aegis of the provincial government, and not under the control of the federal government. This is therefore a resolution declaratory of a principle opposed or adverse to the principle or the provisions of Bill No. C-110.
Moreover, the amendment is not at all on the same plane as the one we proposed last week. In fact last week our amendment was to the effect that the Bank of Canada
Loans to Students
should allow the provinces to take their responsibilities in the field of education, whereas the amendment we put forward today calls for the federal government to hand over to the provinces sources of taxation large enough to allow them to provide students with the necessary scholarships.
The subject matter of the amendment we put forward today is therefore different from that of last week's amendment, since there is no mention of the Bank of Canada, but rather it proposes to use the moneys the federal government would return to the provinces. Therefore, I maintain that our amendment is altogether in accordance with citation No. 382.
Furthermore, the amendment is not, as stated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner), a motion adverse to the provisions of a section of the bill, but rather to the principle of the bill itself, which is to facilitate the making of loans to students.
Since we are against the principle of the bill and, on the contrary, we want scholarships instead of student loans, I believe the amendment is quite in order.

As the hon. member for Lapointe knows, and as the house knows, I am quite happy to argue as to the propriety of an amendment if it is in order, even when I am opposed to it in substance, but it seems to me there is a great deal of similarity between these two amendments. The one moved by the hon. member for Roberval last Thursday asked that the government present new legislation which would authorize the Bank of Canada to supply to the provincial governments the necessary credits to permit them to fulfil completely their responsibilities in the field of education. Now we are asked to support an amendment asking that the government should bring in new legislation with a view to giving the provinces the necessary fiscal revenues to permit them to furnish needed scholarship grants to students.
There are slight differences; the nuances do not compare exactly, but surely the principle is the same. We are being asked not to provide money for student scholarships directly out of the federal treasury but, instead, we are asked to provide the provinces with sufficient financial resources to enable them to fulfil their responsibilities in the field of education.

There is one other citation which might be looked at in this connection. It is citation 194(7) of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which reads:
A motion or amendment cannot be brought forward which is the same in substance as a question which has already been decided, because a proposition being once submitted and carried in the affirmative or negative cannot be questioned again but must stand as the judgment of the house.
I would point out that this citation does not merely speak of amendments which are precisely the same. It suggests that amendments cannot be brought in if they are the same in substance, and I suggest the amendment now proposed is the same in substance as the one we considered on Thursday last.
I was happy on Thursday to support the right of members of the Ralliement Creditiste to bring forward an amendment at the time they did, because I believed it was in order.

Your Honour gave the amendment the benefit of the doubt, and there was later an opportunity to vote on the matter. I would like to speak for a very short time on this bill because it expounds and has inherently in it, elements of reform thinking. It is a reform bill which we are being asked to pass. First, the minister has said that the purpose of this bill is that no student shall be denied a higher education

Loans to Students
merely because he cannot afford it or does not have the financial means. That principle has been spoken of many times in this house on this bill and I will not say anything further on it except that the bill does set the seal of approval of the house on that principle, namely the right to education or education as a right and not an inheritance. Going deeper, beyond that is the statement made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) when he said words to the effect that it is our duty to ensure university education to all those who have the intelligence to acquire it. Hon. members will notice, and I like to think he did this purposely, that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did not say "intelligence and ambition" or "intelligence and drive".
Up to now most of us have considered or have thought of these two attributes of a personality as one thing, ambition and intelligence. These two things are absolutely separate. Many of us, and many others whom we know, have ambition, drive and intelligence, and somehow or other they will make their way to university or get their education. But there are many others who have the intelligence but do not have that drive, that spur driving into them, that dagger that digs into a person's soul and makes him go forward -and yet they are very intelligent. We are losing these people because we have not assured them the education that they could acquire. That is the second principle.
The third principle is by far the most important, and in this respect I am indebted to the right hon. gentleman, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I see that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) is listening very carefully. The Leader of the Opposition said that university education is becoming such a vast and tremendous problem that it now requires national endeavour. I am very obligated to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, because a few weeks ago when I spoke on another bill in connection with education I said that education is now a matter of national concern. I am obliged for that correction, because "concern" is a rather passive thing; it shows interest, but endeavour shows an active interest. I hasten to assure the right hon. gentleman that most people in Canada will agree with him, that education is now a matter of national endeavour and that the only ones who so jealously guard provincial rights, my lord, are the politicians, not the people.

The constitution, Mr. Speaker, is something that is hard to define, but the constitution is not the British North America Act, in my view; an act devised, I might say also, against the better advice of Lord Durham who had put in a fairly good report at that time, in 1843. However, these are the three principles that we find inherent in this bill, whether we like it or not. And this is good. It is the only way we can do it at the present time, because of the restrictions of the British North America Act.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned many difficulties that could be encountered by young people applying for a loan.
I think most of us will agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) that there will be these cases where bankers may not be too willing to lend the money. After all, we have to consider that they are human beings; we are not dealing with angels. I do not think this is criticism, although it is important that we offer constructive criticism so that we will know what we are going to face when we come to it.
If I might go on a little further-and again I should like to assure the minister that what I say is not by way of criticism but in order that we might anticipate these troubles-the first thing which will happen will be that we will not be talking of a loan of $5,000 to a graduate but one more in the neighbourhood of $10,000. Because young men going to university do occasionally marry young ladies at university who bring with them a "dowry" consisting of a $5,000 debt. So we are really talking of $10,000 in such cases. I am reminded of the advice given by Polo-nius to Horatio in Hamlet, when he said: Neither a borrower nor a lender be:
For a loan oft loses both itself and friend, And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
That is advice which most of us should have taken at one time or another, but we

should consider seriously whether we should endow our students with debt. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam knows, it is the intention of all of us eventually to ensure higher education for all who have the intelligence to acquire it. But we have the British North America Act to contend with. I heard the suggestion that it might be better to supply the funds to the Canadian National Railways than to endow more scholarships, but it is difficult to do this without funds. The way we have chosen to do it is by way of loans from banks.
I should like to provide the minister with just as ingenious a method of collecting the money, because we will not find very many friendly people willing to pay back this money. With all due respect to the minister, most young graduates after graduating start to set up a home. Their wages are not that high and a repayment of $800 to $1,000 a year is pretty stiff for them and they will not like us because of it. I can also imagine that many United States concerns will be rushing off to our universities around graduation time offering these young graduates a contract to work for them for five or ten years, and in return these firms will repay the obligation. That will be very enticing, especially when the payments are in U.S. funds. So what we are doing at the present time is leaving it open to the larger concerns to bond these people and tie them up. That is going to happen.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the minister has said that because of these loans both students and country will be the richer. I agree with that, but does it matter to us whether these loans are paid back directly or indirectly, whether by cheque or by payments of income tax? I would offer for the consideration of the minister the suggestion that for a period of 10 years, because of the higher earnings of these students, an amount of $200 or $300 a year be credited them on the loan. Because had it not been for the extra education they received they would have earned only average salaries and paid average income tax; having acquired this education they will be paying more income tax because they can earn more. I think you will see, Mr. Speaker, that as they make more money from year to year they will be paying more by way of income tax, and we should credit the extra payments they are making to the retirement of their debts. They will not object to paying income tax and this method will entice them to stay in Canada rather than move to the United States or elsewhere.

I urge that these students loans for education presently before the house be speedily approved.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) stated last week, Canada's future strength and prosperity depend on our human resour-

ces. I am happy to know that the average student is going to be able to receive help. I do not feel that political patronage exists in Ontario in regard to students looking for bursaries.
As far as I know Peterborough has the newest university in Canada and it will be opening its doors in September. It is on the Trent canal system and is called Trent University. It will be making its mark on our country and will be a tremendous asset to my constituency as well as other areas across Canada. This is one of the reasons why I recommend the passage of this bill to make interest free loans available to students. This legislation should have been brought down earlier in the year. In fact it should have been introduced long before the flag debate was brought before this house so as to enable students to enrol at the usual time. I feel we have lost a year already with this legislation.
Another point I should like to bring up, Mr. Speaker, is that it is of the utmost importance to us to guarantee that our young people graduating from our universities and schools find attractive jobs in Canada so that we do not lose them to the country south of us.
We in Peterborough are proud of our new university, its board of governors and its president. We are proud that the citizens of my constituency have been able to raise $2 million. This money came from industry and its employees, businessmen and the farming community and it is proof of the faith we have in our young people.
I believe the government will have to give further financial help to these institutions. Established universities find it easier to expand because of endowments from ex-students and their families, but this is something on which a new institution cannot depend. The tremendous cost of universities today was outlined in the master plan set up by the president of Trent University in May of this year. The building program over the next 16 years will cost $70 million and the first phase of the plan, which will be completed in 1968, will cost $17 million. I might say that the government of Ontario has committed itself to a big part of this cost, and I should like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) what assistance this government intends to give to new universities. As many speakers before

me have said, this student loans plan is only scratching the surface and the government must plan now for the future financial assistance of new universities.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few comments I want to make on the bill. First of all I wish to register with the minister how very surprised I am to find him bringing in such a weak and anaemic answer to the problem of higher education in Canada. I think the minister is far too intelligent an individual to believe that this measure will really be a very helpful type of contribution, in spite of the many congratulatory speeches that have been made by members from the Toronto and York areas on the matter.
I want to point out first that the loan type of assistance to higher education is possibly the worst type of assistance you can give to people acquiring a higher education. The government of the province of Ontario already has a program of loans for higher education. In many ways the program is a little better than this proposal and in some ways it is perhaps not as good. In the case of Ontario, loans are limited to $500 and as in this instance there is no means test. The student is therefore limited to a maximum of $2,000 up to the time of graduation, but the interest rate is much cheaper, at 4 per cent, and the period of repayment does not commence until a year after graduation. I bring this out simply to point out that there are other loan schemes in existence and that the really significant thing about the Ontario loan scheme is that it has never been oversubscribed. It is a much more modest proposal than the present one, some $3 million, but even though its terms are more favourable the amount provided has never in the history of the scheme been all used.
I was talking the other day to officials of the department of education of Ontario and they were pointing out to me that although the loan provision has never been used to capacity, the bursary and scholarship segment of their program is starved to death for money, that this is where the big demand occurs in higher education, not in the loan field at all but in the field of bursaries and scholarships. This is where the government should be providing assistance. It is significant that in the bill no help is provided 20220-361

in any way at all in the form of scholarships and bursaries and this in spite of the fact that this is the one field in which we know assistance is greatly needed and very much desired.

Two things. First of all, there is the interest rate. The minister told us it is expected that the interest rate will be about 5J per cent. Anybody who has anything to do with bank managers knows very well that they have a limited amount of money to make available for loans each year and they will not lend that money at 52 per cent when it can be lent to commercial customers of the bank at a rate which will earn the bank anywhere from 9 to 11 per cent. Unless the managers have an almost limitless amount of money to lend, and I do not think that will be so, the distribution of the available credit will be to the banks' commercial customers and the money will not be lent to some poor, struggling university student who happens to come along and want a loan at 5| per cent.
I think it is a gross fraud on the public to suggest that by making use of the commercial banks we will have even begun to meet the problem. It would even improve the legislation if the government would at least make cash available to the provinces so they could set up their own loan boards as has been done in some provinces, so that once the student met the qualifications set by the authorities he would know he had a loan and would not have to go shopping around to bank after bank to try to get some bank manager to lend him the money.
I do not want to repeat all of the other criticisms that have been made. It is significant that credit unions are not allowed to participate in this plan. It is significant that there is no provision in the bill for postgraduate work. Yet anyone in the field of education knows that this is one of the vital areas of higher education in Canada. There is a great need for more and more postgraduate work and training. There is nothing in the bill to cover that. There is some provision whereby students can go abroad, but what are you going to do on $1,000 if you want to go, say, to the United States for some sort of postgraduate training.
The criticisms that have been made are not only valid but they tear away the mask of pseudo-Liberalism that surrounds the government. This is another piece of half-baked, weak-kneed legislation that is presented to put up a big front, but the government is not really trying to tackle the problem at all. They are not even intending to put any real money into the scheme. The government is not going to put up any money. They will simply pay the interest rate. Even if the whole $40 million is lent the government will only be contributing something like $2,300,000

or $2,400,000 a year toward higher education in Canada. Again, this is a rather cheap answer to the problem of higher education.
I think one of the most significant speeches made during this debate was made by one of my colleagues the other day in which he pointed out that this government really has not sat down and looked at the problem of higher education at all. All of us who are interested in the field realize that there is not just a crisis in higher education coming in the next 10 or 15 years, there is a nightmare coming. I have a great many clippings here reporting the views of various people in the field of education. They point out the great need for university facilities; the fact that they can hardly accommodate the students who now wish to get a higher education; the lack of teachers, the lack of teacher training; the lack of postgraduate research training. All these things have been drawn to the government's attention in brief after brief. What do we get from them? We get nothing in that line at all, but merely a scheme to try to get more undergraduates into university. This again shows no sense of perspective, no sense of priorities at all.
We know the tremendous sums that are going to have to be expended in the field of education. I spoke last session of the problem of automation alone, and what it is going to do to change our economy. I referred to the massive sums of money which will require to be spent, the magnitude of which I do not believe we can even contemplate at the present time. In the changing world of tomorrow, these questions are going to have to be answered. We have received no indication from this government that they have any understanding of the problem at all. What we really need I suppose in Canada is a federal office of education. This government is in so many fields of education such as technical education, retraining programs, education of Indians, university grants, scholarships through the Canada Council, that what we really need is some method by which the government can begin to give coordination and leadership in the whole field of education. I do not believe you are going to do that until you are prepared to set up a federal office of education.
I know there are constitutional problems involved and I know that one of the provinces in particular objects very strongly to such a proposal being enacted. It is their right to object, and we respect their objections in that regard. However, this does not mean that the other provinces may not wish

We have no intention at all to hinder education. On the contrary, we hope that in the very important field of education, fast progress will be made.
We are also for better understanding between the two main ethnic groups which make up our country. But how will this understanding be attained if the present government continues to act as it has done since it took office, if it continues to undermine the very foundation of the constitution, if it continues to uphold that untenable position as champions of constitutional transgression?

Mr. Speaker, frankly I was very surprised by the attitude of the hon. member for Port Arthur.
In the two years I have been sitting in the house, I saw that hon. member make a few slips but, in general, he behaved like a gentleman. However, after the speech he has just made, I think I have changed my mind for a long time to come.
Mr. Speaker, I would not like to let the debate on Bill No. C-110 pass without making some remarks.
We have been hearing for a long time, Mr. Speaker, that the house will be asked to study a bill enabling all young Canadians to acquire whatever education and vocational training they desire. We were anxiously waiting for that moment which has now arrived. Unfortunately, this bill is far from being what Canadians had a right to expect, since it contains several pitfalls in which our youth will be trapped, sometimes with lifelong consequences, if this bill is adopted in its original form, that is without any amendment.
However, I wish to say right now that I am in favour of the principle of Bill No. C-110, in that it recognizes the necessity of universal education, and also because it states that our educational facilities must be put at the disposal of all those who wish to acquire the required training so as to play their role adequately later on.
Ever since unemployment has taken such alarming proportions in Canada, we have come to realize that most of those who are the more seriously affected are people with less education. We find that situation deplor-20220-362

able and we regret that nothing serious has been done about it earlier.
Even though it is a little late, we admit that assistance should be provided as soon as possible to our young people so that they might receive a better education.
We Creditistes, freedom-loving people, we do not want this measure to be a means to catch young people and involve them in debt for the rest of their life.
Mr. Speaker, every year there is an education week in Canada. Every year the problem of education is looked into, solutions are sought; the need for education is felt and it is acknowledged that everyone is entitled to get an education.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to an editorial published in the newspaper L'Echo Abitibien of March 5, 1964, during the latest week of Canadian education; this editorial states:
Education week provides the opportunity to ponder on the fate of the child. In fact, he is the main character in what can be called the drama of life. It goes without saying, since the future lies in his hands, that the future world will depend of the education which he receives.
Therefore, if the child is the most important being, our main concerns must be centred around him to help him to attain his most perfect development. It is a moving and touching sight to see a child grow.
When he is still very young, one can see his personality emerge and with time passing by the adult of tomorrow slowly emerges. We all hope or should hope that the adult of tomorrow will be up to his heavy responsibilities of which he does not yet suspect the existence but which will be, owing to the force of circumstances, his lot in a not too distant future.
Here is where today's adult comes in. Everyone must give way to the child. Everyone must think of all that will allow the child to develop fully physically, morally and intellectually. All initiatives that tend toward that triple goal are in fact the only ones that really matter.
A lot of time can be spent talking about the number, diversity, quality and scope of those initiatives. Whether they concern the body, soul or mind, they are very useful, because they help train the men of tomorrow. Everyone must do his share in the field which suits him best and he wil certainly be rewarded a hundredfold. If each of us contributes to that great task which is to prepare the child to take over, he will surely have put into practice the theme of the week: Education, human contact.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether in bringing forward Bill No. C-110 the government takes into consideration the value of the child, of young men and young girls and what is expected from them in years to come.
With the ever spreading belief in all circles, that everybody is entitled to education, the Minister of Finance of the Liberal government

introduced Bill No. C-110, an act to facilitate the making of loans to students.
When reading the bill, Mr. Speaker, I was reminded of the story of the little boy who came running home, all excited, shouting to his mother: "Quick, quick, my little brother is stuck in the mud." The mother hurried along and asked: "Did he sink in deeply?" And the little boy answered: "Up to his ankle." Then the mother said: "Now, there 'S no need to hurry or get excited, there is no danger, it is nothing serious." But the little boy replied: "He fell in head first."
This Bill No. C-110 will have exactly the same effect of sinking in the mud for the rest of their days all the students who will avail themselves of this legislation.
Our farmers have been pushed into debt for the rest of their life. The workers were indebted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the rest of their days. As to small industries and small businessmen, they are also loaded with debts for a lifetime. The fishermen also will struggle with debts for the rest of their lives.
Now, our future professional people are also to be loaded with a debt for life. They were about the only ones who were not directly affected by this debt money system which has burdened us for years-a heritage of the old political parties, Grit or Tory.
By means of this bill our students are to be stuck head first in this mire of debts, grappling with chartered banks.
This bill is submitted to us in order to help the students. However, the students will soon find out that the bill is not so much to help them but rather those who control the nation's credit and money, that is the chartered banks.
The students themselves do not want such regimentation, such invasion of the educational field, by the federal government, and for very good reasons.
During Canadian education week, which I mentioned earlier, Mr. Maurice Huot, editorialist of Le Droit, wrote on March 4, 1964:
It has been repeated again and again, and not without reason, that greater learning will be needed to take one's place efficiently in tomorrow's, and even today's, society. Yet, as I say, education should not be confused with training. While dispensing practical knowledge, teachers must Impart the art of living within society, while respecting and serving others. That is education in its highest sense.
We must not only prepare our young people to earn a dollar in exchange for professional services, but also to become useful citizens, complete citizens in their immediate community.

The bill now before us will bring about precisely the opposite of what Maurice Huot, Le Droit's editorialist, was asking for, in that it will take our young people and turn them into sharks at the service of bankers who will suck the few dollars they will receive from society.
What will happen when the student has graduated, if he takes advantage of the legislation now proposed to us? He will have a debt of $5,000. Besides living and organizing his business office, he will have to repay that $5,000 debt plus the interest.
Who will have to pay for that? It will be the client, the consumer; always the consumer.
This bill will induce our graduates to become money collectors at the service of bankers.
More and more streams of protests are coming from the province of Quebec. I hope that the premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, will not become an accomplice of the federal government to sell freedom of education to his Ottawa centralizing friends, as was done in the past by another Quebec premier, a premier who, during the last war, sold Quebec fiscal rights; and we all know the problems that followed in our province.
In the province of Quebec, people are now wondering what the premier and the provincial government are doing in view of the centralizing tendency of this bill by the federal Liberal government.
We have fought from the early days of the colony to maintain our rights, our faith, our language and our traditions. We always had to stand in the breach, prepared to drive back those who, through the years, attempted to take away from us what we held most dear.
If this bill is passed, we will see the central government enter a field which does not concern it at all. Yet, when we consider what is happening in this country at the present time, all that is lacking in Canada, all that we have to develop and that Canadians are asking for, and which concerns the federal government, we realize that ministers, and especially the Minister of Finance, would have much to do, particularly in the field of finance, without interfering with matters that do not concern them.
The minister who brought forth this bill certainly did not make a great effort. He was badly inspired or ill advised. I see that this Bill No. C-110 was prepared hastily during a discussion on the flag. The flag question was debated one, two or three days and, during

that time the bill was prepared. When they are exhausted they revert to the flag. The flag question is discussed in our spare time. It gives them time to prepare something else. If the minister had tried a little, he would easily have found a liberating legislation instead of legislation likely to get tomorrow's youth into debt.
For many years, and especially since 1962, there has been a real Creditiste group in the house.
We are suggesting to the government a way to free itself from the masters of finance, to free the country from debt and taxes which are a heavy burden on the people and prevent Canada from developing as it should. The government has always turned a deaf ear on our claims. Instead of considering their logic, it introduces legislation to be administered by a system which will get Canadians more and more into debt and prevent the country from developing as it should.
It is mostly those for whom this bill is intended who are against it. Last week the hon. member for Roberval received a protest telegram from the president of the students of the University of Montreal. I have here a letter dated July 15 last, that is last week, addressed to Mr. Gilles Gregoire, member for Lapointe, Ottawa. I should like to quote from this letter in order to show how much the students are against this bill as put forward today. I quote:

The Laval University students' union is strongly against Bill No. C-110 now being discussed by the House of Commons.
Any federal venture in the field of education is an offence against the constitution. How can you ask young people and especially separatists to respect confederation when federal ministers are making a mockery of it. The interest to be paid by the federal government on student loans constitutes a grant to students and, as such, is unconstitutional. Even the proposed compensation formula cannot satisfy us. Only the complete absence of the federal government will.
That compensation formula was arrived at because the total sum of the interest paid on $12 million in loans would amount to $720,000, which would represent for our province a recovery of 0.1 per cent of the federal tax. We agree that such a recovery would not constitute a very practical solution.

Mr. Speaker, this shows that the students of the province of Quebec particularly are against the intrusion of the federal government in provincial fields. We have a constitution that precludes the federal government from intruding in the field of education, in provincial jurisdictions.
Mr. Speaker, we want to have that respected; we ask the government to respect that.
That is why, for my part, I am against this bill in its present form. I am surprised to note the position taken by the Conservatives last week and today with regard to this bill.
Last week especially I was not too surprised at the fact that Conservative members from Quebec were against the bill. Of course the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bal-

cer) came out practically in favour of the bill, but he spoke almost in a whisper, as if he were ill at ease.
However, the other members spoke against the principle of the bill. On the other hand, when the time came for them to take positive action so as to show how serious they were, all Conservative members voted against the amendment, the purpose of which was precisely to give the provinces the freedom of action to which they are entitled in the field of education.
Mr. Speaker, if the government wants to administer the affairs of the people properly, to respect provincial autonomy and the freedom of the citizens, to respect democracy as we are told, it has but one thing do to, and that is give instructions to the Bank of Canada to make available to the provinces the necessary capital, without interest, so as to permit them to administer their affairs in the best interests of their people and of the Canadian nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot let the vote be taken on Bill No. C-110 without expressing briefly my personal feelings, those of my constituents and those of my province in this respect.
Opposite I see the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne). In my opinion, he must be happy since the debate on this bill allows us to witness the most crucial demonstration of what is known as co-operative federalism.
We had co-operative federalism concerning loans to municipalities and the pension plan. We spoke about co-operative federalism when several social security measures were discussed, for instance an increase in the allowances for 16 and 17 year olds. But today, Mr. Speaker, we see co-operative federalism and we speak about it in a field which touches the very heart of Quebeckers, that is education.
I know very well that in some jurisdictions jointly exercised with the provinces, it was possible for several premiers to gather around a table and discuss whether there was some way to reach a compromise for the greater advantage of all Canadians. I understand this very well in a field of joint jurisdiction, but if the federal government presents legislation concerning education directly, I wonder how, with the support of 45 or 50 members from the province of Quebec who enable it to govern the country, it can possibly expect all the members to approve it simply because the legislation benefits the students.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, thought for a while that the Quebec students would say: We were in need of this legislation.
I, too, in my youth, got an education and was short of money. If, at that time, somebody had told me: Here is $1,000 from the federal government, I seriously wonder if I would not have accepted it. The reaction of the Quebec university students taught me that nowadays, the young people say: Of course, we need money, but we shall get it where the government can give it to us according to the constitution.
I was listening the other day to one of my colleagues speak on the constitutional aspect of Bill No. C-110. He said: I cannot understand how a certain province-it was the province of Quebec-maintains that this bill violates the constitution. After all, the students will be able to choose the professor they want, even the university; they will be able to choose the bank they want and even to apply or not for a loan.
If you listen to that line of reasoning, you are inclined to say: That is true, we are making a fuss about nothing, we are frightening ourselves unduly for, after all, what can that take away from us?
At that time the practical point of view was being examined by one of my colleagues. On the other hand, if you keep up the same line of reasoning, you could tell yourself: When the federal government talked about increasing the allowance to young people 16 and 17 years old still going to school, what was it after all? Just an extension of social allowances to young people 16 and 17 years old. We will let the bill pass because after all it takes away none of Quebec's rights.
Today we are asked to approve legislation providing for student loans and some people will say: "What does it matter? After all, one will submit an application only if one wishes to do so, and one will attend the university of his choice and study under the teacher one wants. That will take nothing away from the provinces."
But, Mr. Speaker, what will stop the federal government if tomorrow it decides to start paying the teachers in the provinces? One could still say: "I can choose the teacher I want and the school board does not have to accept those grants. We will continue teaching languages, religion and traditions, so what is the difference?" Later on what would prevent the federal government from presenting a bill to build universities? Then, we could say: Who would stop the provinces from accepting it, since the provincial and

the university authorities would be able to select their professors and the subject matters they want to be taught? What does it matter? This means that after the four pieces of legislation submitted by the federal government are passed, the provinces would not need their department of education any longer.
I am not oblivious of the fact that we always look rather foolish when we object to the federal government infringing upon the provincial field. But co-operative federalism could not find a field that would hurt more the provinces generally, and Quebec in particular, than that of education.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I might have been prepared to support this measure if it had involved, once again, equalization. For example, in the field of social security, we, from the province of Quebec, have this to say: This field belongs to us, but we understand that the central government must be strong, that it has to draw upon the richer provinces' funds to help the poorer provinces. Up to a point we are prepared to accept that principle.
If this bill was, in effect, to say to the provincial authorities of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Newfoundland: Your universities are poor and we are going to ask the representatives from Ontario, British Columbia or Quebec to help your students pay their university fees, we would have said: This is contrary to the constitution, but we are going to discuss it, because the federal government has at least one reason namely, that the rich provinces should help the poor ones.
But as far as the bill before us is concerned, this matter is not even being considered, as we are going to grant exactly the same amount, per capita, to the university students. As a matter of fact, it means that should $800,000 be taken from the province of Quebec for education purposes, it is to be expected that $800,000 will go to Quebec. It is also to be expected that should $200,000 be taken from Newfoundland, an amount of $200,000 will be paid to Newfoundland.
All this makes me wonder where the government is going. They are going to take $10 from Quebec in order to lend $10 to that province. They are going to get $10 from Newfoundland so as to lend it to Newfoundland students. They are going to borrow $10 from Ontario so as to lend it afterwards to an Ontario student.
But what the deuce is the government doing there?
