It would be so easy for the Quebec provincial authorities to go and get $10 within the limits of the province and give that $10 back to the province of Quebec.
It would be easy for the Newfoundland government to go and get $10 within its boundaries and give that $10 back to the province, and the same can be said about Ontario. The government of that province could collect that amount of $10 and give it to Ontario students.
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised, I fail to see what the federal government is doing in a field which comes exclusively under the provincial jurisdiction, when it has decided to distribute these loans on a basis proportional to the population of the province and when we know very well that it is going to collect that money in the province concerned. I am wondering why we should talk of co-operative federalism in this case when it is not relevant at all? Why should we talk of equalization, which is not even mentioned here? It is simply a new intrusion of the federal government upon a field in which it has no concern.
And why do we have those intrusions? Simply because during an electoral campaign, when minds see things with excitement, it seems in order to say all over Canada: We will provide $1,000 student loans. Such a statement brings in votes. But when the time came to pass that legislation, it is realized that one has interfered where one had no right to interfere. And today, Bill No. C-110 is submitted to us.
I listened this afternoon to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) answering the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). He had this to say: In fact, Mr. Jean Lesage was present at the federal-provincial conference and it seems to me that he can speak for his province.
Mr. Speaker, I maintain that when constitutional rights are at stake, neither a premier, a provincial leader of the opposition, nor the prime minister, or the cabinet, or the federal government has the right to go against that constitution. In a democracy, under a free system, the only thing the people really control is their constitution.
It would be so easy for the 10 premiers to meet and say: "We are going to accept this measure."
From a political standpoint it is a very good thing for the government to grant subsidies and extend loans. It is even a very good thing for Mr. Jean Lesage to come to a federal-provincial conference and state: "All

Loans to Students
right, give it to all the other provinces; as for me, I will take my share and do whatever I want with it in my own province."
It is very good from a political standpoint. But neither Mr. Jean Lesage, Mr. Robarts, nor Mr. Roblin, in short no premier has the power to come to Ottawa for a federal-provincial conference and amend the constitution. Nobody has such a right. Only the people have this right, because the constitution belongs to them.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of my remarks,
I am proud to say that I share the feelings of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) who stated, when he dealt with the matter of federal-provincial relations: "It is the priority rights which are important."
As far as I am concerned, and though it might upset some hon. members, I must say that I do not believe in the priority needs of the provinces. As a matter of fact, what are the priority needs of a province?
Each province thinks it has priority needs. For Quebec, it is education; for another province it may be mining, and for another again there is the labour problem. What is a priority need, if not what a province lacks?
Personally, I believe in priority rights, it is a principle which I shall defend to the last. And what are the priority rights of a province? They stem from what a few people decided, about a century ago, when they said: If we want a greater Canada, minorities must be protected. Now, if we want to protect the minorities, the federal government must have certain responsibilities, and so must the provincial governments. When these responsibilities were being apportioned, education went to the provinces, because it is the very basis of culture, the protector of language, creed and traditions. And, today, by very devious, very subtle means, the federal government introduced two bills concerning provincial rights and educational matters.
The first piece of legislation provided for school allowances for 16 and 17 years old students. There are those who might tell me: The provinces have, for a long time, accepted the principle of family allowances. That is true. But whether disguised or not, the principle of school allowances for young people 16 and 17 years old was not discussed when the provinces handed over their powers to the federal government. And, even if they had, Bill No. C-110 which is before us today goes even further. Loans will be made to students.
Mr. Speaker, if I were asked how I shall vote on this matter, I should hardly know
[Mr. Girouard.l
the answer. Because Mr. Lesage came to Ottawa and said: "Very well, grant these loans to students in other provinces, but give me the money and I shall dispose of it as I please."
At first sight it seemed all right to say that the federal government did not meddle with any of our prerogatives, that provinces were free to do as they pleased. But what was overlooked, what Mr. Lesage did not realize, is that he was at the same time agreeing to a breach of the constitution. He forgot that it was his responsibility, as premier of a province, to defend the rights of his province and to safeguard the constitution, even if he wanted all students in Canada to get subsidies or loans to continue their schooling.
A member of the Ralliement Creditiste said that those students would become sharks at the service of the bank, and that they would in turn eat up the poor people. Mr. Speaker, such an assertion is false, because when a student has completed his course and wishes to charge a rate which may seem extravagant to some people, he deserved it in full. I would not wish to put forward a personal example, but if the hon. member who preceded me would look at my life history, he would realize that our studies are dearly paid for, and earned the hard way, but that once we become professionals, we are not necessarily sharks at the service of financiers or bankers.
Mr. Speaker, I must stand against Bill No. C-110, even if that should displease several hon. members, because we did not object to school allowances for 16 and 17 year old people. In fact, the majority of hon. members do not seem to object to the granting of loans to students by the federal government. I would go as far as to say that nine provinces out of 10 would like the government to set up a department of education.
Well, if nine provinces out of 10 agreed to let the federal government establish a federal department of education, I would approve that attitude, because it would show definitely that a tenth province does not want it, a province which is different from the others, and to which a special status must be granted in order to keep it within confederation.
That is just about what the province of Quebec is claiming, because the province of Quebec has special things to preserve, such as its language, its faith and its traditions. As soon as our English speaking colleagues understand that there are two great nations living side by side in this country, the

English and the French nations, and that they cannot compromise on certain subjects, we will finally be able to establish a strong confederation.
Let us give special status to the province of Quebec and continue confederation. Then, things will be perfect and I will not accuse my provincial premier, Mr. Jean Lesage, of coming to Ottawa to become the accomplice of the Liberal government and sell rights belonging to his province under the constitution. I shall simply say that we have a special status.
If such legislation can be useful to the rest of Canada, I agree. This may appear contradictory to you, Mr. Speaker, but personally I am in favour of a strong central government. I want it to be strong, but in its own field, just like I want the provinces to be strong, but in their own field.
Some hon. members have asked me "When will that stop? When will the province of Quebec stop these recriminations? When will these representations stop?"
The answer is simple. I told them: "This will stop merely by complying with the constitution; if, for years, the federal government has unceasingly encroached upon provincial rights, it is still possible to settle the situation, by reverting to the constitution. If they do not want to go back to the constitution because it might displease the English speaking provinces or weaken them economically, let us then give a special status to the province of Quebec and, once again the case would be settled. We will still have a confederation, with a strong central government; we will have several provinces willing to surrender many of their rights to a central government, while the province of Quebec will have retained its exclusive powers over which it keeps a jealous watch.
This, Mr. Speaker, is my personal opinion.
I say once again that the members have to stand up in the house to remind the federal government that, even though social legislation and loans to students may be politically profitable, we happen to live in a confederation in which were admitted, in all good faith, as many people from Lower Canada as there were from Upper Canada because then, everyone hoped and believed that their respective rights would be protected, although I feel that the present government, with its co-operative federalism, is undermining the very foundation of our country for many years to come.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to Bill No. C-110, I should like to point out to hon. members that without the Creditistes in this house I wonder where the country would be, because the new measures introduced these last few years tend to centralize and to specialize everything at an alarming rate. What we want is to legislate in terms of human beings, while preserving their present and future freedom.
I shall vote against this bill, because I claim that education concerns the provinces primarily and we are in favour of the autonomy of the provinces.
Let us imagine, for instance, a young man of 18 who wants to complete his studies by means of a federal loan. What will he do at 23 when he finds himself with a $5,000 debt, with all the other debts he will have to incur at that age, namely those resulting from marriage, rent, furniture, car, etc.?
I say that instead of doing a service to the students, this is putting them in debt for their whole lifetime and may discourage them for several years.
If the government truly wishes to assist students, let it give scholarships and favour free education by allowing the Bank of Canada to grant interest free loans to the provinces in that connection. Thus, the problem would be solved once and for all.
The province of Quebec has promised free education, but since it is deep in debt it can hardly get any credit nowadays and delays the implementation of that promise.
If the central government determined once and for all the role of the Bank of Canada, interest free loans could be granted to the provinces and all the people of Canada would benefit from them.
Instead of supporting capitalists, we would work to give to the future generation a very serious token. We would thus train learned and educated men who would do credit to Canada and could begin their career free of debt. Thus, the governor of the Bank of Canada would not have to warn the people to live within their means and to tighten their purse strings, as did Mr. Coyne a few years ago.

Consumers are not to blame, but the gov-erment is. The pieces of legislation submitted to us would compel people to run into debt and become fettered. No, Mr. Speaker, we want to get rid of the fetters of federal legislation.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at six o'clock, I was saying that instead of helping our students, our youth, the present government is rather trying by all available means to lull them with certain programs which will lead nowhere.
We have received protests from several universities of the province of Quebec, to the

effect that students are not willing to accept the federal government's proposition and that they even request the house to reject Bill No. C-110.
It is not that students would not need some money to complete their studies, but they are looking further ahead. They know that they are the ones who will, in the long run, have to foot the bill. Our present governments are mortgaging the future of our youth and the future of generations ahead.
Instead of settling problems, the government is putting off their settlement, without bringing forward any solutions which would allow it to meet its responsibilities. That is why we, in this corner of the house, are against those half measures which are invariably brought before us.
In conclusion, I will read a letter from the general student association of the University of Sherbrooke. We have also received such a letter from the student association of the University of Montreal and one from the association of the University of Quebec. I quote:
Sherbrooke, July 17, 1964.
We are anxious to join our colleagues of the Universities of Montreal and Quebec to show our disapproval of your bill concerning loans to students.
We object to this system for various reasons. First, there is a gross violation by the federal government of the provincial jurisdiction with regard to sections 92 and 93 of our Canadian constitution. Our second objection is that this project is but another alleged remedy to make university education available to all.
With this project, you are simply mortgaging the taxpayers of tomorrow. You hide behind a smokescreen the real problem, which is the setting up of free education, the only solution to a free access to university. Here, in Quebec, the government in office promised us free education and we want it to be put into effect as soon as possible. This is why your project cannot be accepted.
The only thing that would seem acceptable, would be a system of free scholarships. This would amount to the same thing as free education.
Yours sincerely,
And this letter is signed by Pierre Hogue, president.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to detain the house only a few minutes, but I did want to deal with one or two aspects of this problem that have not been mentioned to date. Like my colleagues I support the purpose of the bill. However my colleagues have pointed out its shortcomings on several grounds. I am not going to repeat those at this time-I think they have been very well placed before the house-but
Loans to Students
I wish to point out one other shortcoming that I think has not been mentioned. It is that in obtaining a B.A. or B.Sc. a student would have accumulated quite a body of debt. Having to face the repayment of that debt, that student's or graduate's opportunities for postgraduate work might be denied or might be unduly postponed. I suggest that aspect of the question should receive some consideration.
However, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with one or two of the broader aspects of education, shall I say the philosophy of education, in reply to the remarks of a few of our colleagues in the extreme, geographically located left wing of the chamber, but politically right wing of the chamber. I was very interested in the references they made on occasion. I hope they will take these remarks most kindly, because I think they are really a very nice group of people as individuals; it is only in their collective aspect that we oppose them. Several times these colleagues of ours in the Creditiste group referred to the influence of this bill on students in Quebec, as if it may influence them in the wrong direction or cause them to forget their loyalty to their French culture, and so on. I must point out to them that their minister of education was a Rhodes scholar, and Cecil Rhodes granted these scholarships to any man who would promote the welfare of the empire. The minister of education took advantage of one of those scholarships and went to Oxford. There he came under the influence of the Oxford University atmosphere, with all that that implies and means. Then, I am reliably informed, he wrote his thesis on "Federalism in the empire". Then he returned to Quebec, and I am quite sure the minister of education's attitude to life now completely belies the argument of the hon. gentlemen who suggest that if a student from Quebec accepts some funds as a result of the passage of this bill, he will be influenced, shall I say, to some extent in the wrong direction.
I want to deal with one or two other aspects of this matter. Some of my colleagues are inclined to think that I live emotionally in the Victorian period; that is, only for short periods. But anyway, in the Victorian period there were three fallacies accepted by many intelligent and well meaning reformers. I think the first was that progress was inevitable; the second was that education was a cure-all for the ills of mankind; and the third was that education was the antidote for barbarism. I want to deal with that topic for a few minutes. Since that romantic period, shall I say, we have experienced the greatest,

Loans to Students
officially sponsored barbarism in the history of the world, supported by some of the most highly trained people in the world at that time from the various universities of Europe. We must not forget-I will round out my argument later-that a very high percentage of the officers in Hitler's elite guard had a doctor's degree and quite a number of them had degrees in economics. I am not sure if it was in hydro economics, Mr. Speaker, but they had degrees in economics, philosophy, and so on. Also some of the very best minds of France supported the proposals for the downfall of French democracy prior to 1939; and I find from correspondence and discussions with people who have just returned from conversations with leading people in the United States that even in the United States today Senator Goldwater has a lot of support from persons who have had the greatest possible advantages as far as higher education is concerned.
I was talking to a graduate only this morning, a freshman from one of the eastern universities. I will not mention the name of the university because I do not want to embarrass the members from that province. The president gave an address to the freshmen students at the last opening of the school year, and that address revolved around two points. First, the great advantages and virtues of the city in which the university was situated; second, the value of a degree in dollars. The university president I was told actually had a chart on the wall of his office to show what a B.A. was worth, or a B.Sc., or an M.A., or an M.Sc., or a doctor of philosophy, and so on. But not one word was there in this address to these students with respect to making a contribution to Canadian national life.
I had another experience, Mr. Speaker. Some friends wrote to me from the district from which I come, and they told me that there were some students from the University of British Columbia carrying around a petition urging the government of British Columbia to grant more funds to the University of British Columbia for buildings, and they were asking people to sign this petition. It was a very good cause which we supported. But these people made a point about this. They arranged with several dozen others to ask the students the question: What is your purpose in obtaining a university education? In 90 per cent of the cases the answer was: To make more money. I just bring this to the attention of the house so that hon. members will realize that we have work to do in this connection.
As far as I can see there are three major objectives nowadays with regard to students. The first is the purely material one-to make more money. This is not their fault; it is ours because of the philosophy of life which has been adopted. That is the society in which we live. The second is to secure intellectual competence. Very often that competence is combined with an intellectual arrogance. That is where we get our administrators from, and some of them are in the civil service. These people are highly trained, yet divorced from an understanding of people. Then we get the third group-and I will not underestimate its numbers or influence-comprising those students who accept a university education as an opportunity to make a contribution to Canadian national life, welfare and progress. And that is the purpose and spirit of this bill.
Why is this understanding lacking today after years and years of bitter experiences in the recent history of the world which we are witnessing every day? You cannot pick up a paper these days, Mr. Speaker, without seeing some cause for friction, and in some cases for bloodshed, between various groups in the world. I submit the reasons are twofold. First of all the morals of the society in which we live, which are dog eat dog morals plastered over with a superficial layer of professed Christianity on the part of those who support the system. The second reason is that we have failed to stress the fact that education without moral perception is a hollow shell; there is no question about that. We can train engineers, economists, administrators, managers and so on; but unless that training is coupled with moral perception, as I said before, then in my opinion it is a hollow shell. That has been demonstrated repeatedly since the early days of this century.
I want to quote a passage or two to illustrate the shallowness and lack of understanding and knowledge on the part of many persons who are educated in one particular field but are without an over-all, total approach to life. I have before me the transcript of a radio broadcast given over CHQM of Vancouver on July 3, and it says this:
People who worry about Canada's image in other countries must have been horrified at a report from Seattle this week.
The report-carried by the Sun-outlined the results of a survey taken at a convention in Seattle to test the knowledge and opinion that American delegates had of Canada.
Very few of those questioned came even close to passing the test in a manner likely to please any red-blooded Canadian.

Mind you, Mr. Speaker, this was a conference of educators in the United States, top people in that field.
The report said there was fairly general agreement that Canada was "up north" and a rather decent neighbour to the United States-but beyond that the lact of the most elementary knowledge abou Canada was depressing.
Such informal surveys have been taken before among Americans by Canadian newspapers, with somewhat similar results.
The astonishing thing about this survey, however, is that the people questioned could not be classed as average American citizens, who understandably are often preoccupied with their own overwhelming domestic affairs.
The objects of this survey were delegates to the convention of the U.S. national education association. They were teachers, members of a profession who should be more aware of the "outside" world than the results of the survey indicated.
And if they aren't all experts on international matters, it shouldn't be too much to expect them to at least have some basic knowledge about Canada -which, after all, is the United States' best trading customer, closest ally, and more intimate culturally and socially with the United States than any other nation.
The one thing Canadians have learned from this survey is this: If American teachers are so lacking in information about Canada, we can hardly expect the so-called "average" American to know much about us.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, to indicate the ignorance which can exist among persons who, we presume, are highly trained and educated. And the same situation exists to some extent in Canada. I am not talking down to people. I do not profess to be an educated person. I can read and write and carry on in that way, and that is the reason I have been able to follow these matters. But people are interested in education; I can tell that from letters I receive and conversations I have with people who are interested in real education; an education for a total view of life with human overtones.
Now what do we need? In my opinion we need some leadership, Mr. Speaker. However before I deal with that I want to quote briefly an editorial which indicates this sort of lack of understanding of the need for this type of education. I want to quote from the Saturday, July 18 issue of the Globe and Mail, an editorial which starts off in this way:
When the Canadian home and school and parent-teachers federation held its annual meeting at Winnipeg last year, it had before it a proposal to mark Canada's 1967 centennial with an international conference of parents and teachers.
Mr. C. Max Bedford, national president, said the purpose of the 1967 meeting would be to promote international peace, understanding and co-operation. "This is a shrinking world, facing the possibility of nuclear annihilation, and we feel we have the moral responsibility to attempt it".
Loans to Students
The suggestion was approved with only three dissenting votes. The 1967 rally was given an official title, the world conference of parents and teachers. In January of this year, however, anticommunist pressures began to make themselves felt. The organizers of the conference started wondering out loud if they should invite, delegates from Russia, China, Poland, Czechoslovakia, etc.
This week as the Canadian home and school and PT federation held its annual meeting at Charlottetown, the anti-communist pressure emerged and identified itself as American. Officials of the national parent-teacher association in the United States said that if any communist countries were represented at the Ottawa conference, the United States would boycott it.
The U.S. delegate to the Charlottetown meeting. Mr. Ralph Frost of Knoxville, Tenn., said that communist representatives "would not be representing actual parent-teacher groups, but would be agents of totalitarian governments"...
In the end, the Canadian home and school officials yielded to U.S. fears and threats. Mr. Bedford said that the Ottawa conference would be held without any communist representation: a world conference with one third of the world excluded. Otherwise, he said, it would have to be scrapped completely.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, to indicate the shallowness of mind of some people who are supposed to be interested in education. Our government officially is in favour of cultural contacts between these various countries and is in favour of trading with them. Yet a reputable organization in this country yields, shall I say, to the anti-intellectual approach of those people who do not want a world congress on this basis but want these other countries limited. Who could work more efficiently to promote understanding of our different educational systems than the educators in question and the parent-teachers association of Canada?
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, people are interested in education and they are interested in the bill now before us, even with all the imperfections that have been mentioned by our leader and other members of our group. But there must be leadership in this direction in Canada if we are going to get the value out of education that we hope to get. We need leadership from governments. We need better leadership from the universities and the leaders of our universities who in my opinion are not doing their share to direct attention to the type of education required to meet modern circumstances and conditions. There are still too many of our leading university people who are afraid to say what they think in case they offend the government and, let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that happens in my own province of British Columbia. We need a national purpose and a national policy in Canada with respect to education. I do not

Loans to Students
mean control of education by the federal government, but we need to coalesce our ideas and have some target to present to our young people in the form of a national purpose as the result of federal-provincial co-operation and university co-operation. We need a policy associated with that purpose.
We need to teach our young people the reason for education. The reason for education is not simply to make money, although higher standards of living naturally flow from education and are radiated to the other sections of the community. We need a philosophy in this country upon which to found a sound educational system. We need an understanding of history and our young people need to have an understanding of our democratic and parliamentary institutions. We need legislation as part of a national plan to this effect and not just a tidbit such as this bill, which is introduced as a bits and bobs piece of legislation. We do this in this direction. We will pass a Canada pension plan, we hope, in the near future. We pass other pieces of legislation. But it is all unrelated. What we should have is a national plan and a national target in all these respects.
I see you looking rather darkly at me, Mr. Speaker. I want to say in conclusion that we can easily train multitudes to be clever in one field, as administrators, as engineers and as scientists, as docile servants of a self-seeking society, or we can train human beings whose moral perception will cause them to make their contribution toward the building of a Canada for the full enjoyment of all Canadians in association with all people who have similar ideas. I have got this off my chest, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to sit down.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on the bill but after some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) concerning the left-wingers on the Liberal skating rink, as it might be called, I should like to say a few words with regard to the ideas he put forward, so that there will not be any misunderstanding as to our position in respect of the bill and why we introduced an amendment the other day to give more control to the provinces so that they would have a greater say in the educational system.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned that our minister of education in Quebec received some of his education under a system similar to that incorporated in the bill. I must say that the minister of education
[Mr. Herridge.l
of Quebec is probably more socialist than some socialists themselves. If you want an example of that I would point out that he even established a trusteeship over the Jacques Cartier school board in Montreal, and I must say I do not agree with the basis on which he established it. Because he is the minister of education does not mean that most of the people in the province of Quebec agree with his political ideas.
We must remember one thing. The government serves or guides the nation. That is their role, but very often the nation has to serve as the government's fool's railing so that they do not turn aside from their course too often. I believe that at times the people have to have their say so that the government will open their eyes to the fact that they are straying pretty far. We got rid of state control when we got rid of imperialism in France and in England. Louis XIV said, "The state is I". That was rather far fetched, but I imagine he had strong control. This is exactly the trap that the people of Canada as well as those of other nations may fall into today. The people did not vote for kings, but they do not vote for bureaucrats either. When the state lines up people, everybody lines up one behind the other, but the fact is that the people want to have more say. They revolted against such control during the French revolution against the king and they will revolt against any sort of state control if it is carried to extremes.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West when he says we should have more state control or that the federal government should have more to say with regard to the control and administration of education. This is one domaine, one field of activity that belongs to the provinces. First of all, the most important government you can have in a country is the family itself. That is the basic cell of any nation and if you rip open that basic cell you are ripping open the whole nation. You are actually taking away more and more by government legislation the powers of the mother and father over the family. It is not in the power of the government to do so either in this country or in any other.
The closest authority to the family and to the children themselves is found in the municipality and the school board. They have more to say and should have more to say about the educational system than the government of a province or even the federal government. Yet today the governments of some of the provinces, such as the province of Quebec, are trying to curtail more and more the hold

of the school boards over the educational system. In the province of Quebec they have even lost control of 70 per cent of their budgets and only control 30 per cent now. Yet the federal government wants to control another portion. This is not according to the basic principles of democracy under which we want the people to decide for themselves and not the state. The people may vote for a government. They vote for a man, yes, but they do not vote for bureaucrats. You do not vote for things that you do not control. With the bill now before us we are tending to take away from the people some of their say with regard to the education of their children.
This does not concern only the province of Quebec, but all the provinces of Canada. I say what is good for the other provinces is good for Quebec. But if you are going to give the provinces something, please leave them at least with the freedom and privilege to do as they please in the exercise of these rights and as they feel should be done for the benefit of all the people. The ones who are closest to the people are the ones who know their troubles. I can say right now that the federal government is going farther and farther away from the people. This is one field of activity into which the federal government should not poke its nose for fear it might mess it up, as they have messed up some other fields of activity.
If the federal government wants to be helpful in the educational field, they can give some guidance, yes, but they cannot impose their will. They can help the nation by helping the provinces first of all. The province has its own educational system. Let the provinces decide for themselves. They can decide this better than we can here. They know what is good for them. They have their own traditions, their own needs and their own educational systems. Let them decide for themselves. If we want to be helpful, we can give them some financial help, but let us not try to put a collar over the students. Let there be no control that way, because we are too far away from the people to start deciding what they should study in school.
We were not born yesterday. You can say that politics does not play a game like that. You might find some people gullible enough to believe that politicians do not play that game, but you will not find everyone in this country that gullible, that's for sure. This is one time the federal government might start respecting the provinces by leaving this educational field to the provinces. This is one thing the late John F. Kennedy said which
Loans to Students
might be applied here, if one broadens the sense of the remark. He said, do not ask what your country can do for you, but ask what you can do for your country. I am speaking to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) at the moment and I say the best thing he can do for this country is to keep his nose out of this business and let the provinces solve their own problems. If the federal government wants to be charitable to the provinces, they will not try to solve their problems because they will only make them greater.
I agree that the province of Ontario has financial needs, as do the western provinces and the eastern provinces. I think the federal government has been digging into the pockets of the citizens of Canada because that is the only treasury they have. It is true the federal government can help financially by giving some money back to the provinces, but not by giving it to the people directly. I honestly believe that this is something entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces and for that reason I cannot support this bill any more than my colleagues can. The provinces were given jurisdiction in this field a long time ago, so let us leave it with them.
I regret to say that sometimes the leader of the New Democratic party says we should bring jurisdiction back to Ottawa. When he was a member of a provincial government in 1944 he said jurisdiction should be left with Regina. He has been travelling back and forth. When he has been in Ottawa he wants jurisdiction in Ottawa; when he is in Regina he wants jurisdiction in Regina. This is understandable. This is his idea, and I respect it, but that does not mean that I accept. I believe this government is overstepping its rights and getting into something they have no business being in at all. The jurisdiction belongs with the provinces and we should leave it there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the Minister of Finance speaks now, he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if hon. members would permit me, before dealing with this debate, to try to clear up a mystery that has developed in the parliamentary restaurant concerning a missing cake? I understand it was the birthday of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Watson), and I am sure we all wish him well. A cake was produced and was delivered but because of some confusion in names the cake was de-

Loans to Students
livered to the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker), who was having a party. He ate it. I wish to assure the hon. member for Assiniboia that this was not a case of partisanship. We hope he will have his cake tomorrow. If another cake can be produced tomorrow, we will all help him eat it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to some very interesting speeches for several days. From the many things that so many hon. members have said, I have rather gathered the impression that the majority of the members of this house are planning to support this bill. I say this despite the number of people who have given the impression that they are going to oppose it. The spokesmen for several of the parties have said it is their intention to support this bill. However some of their supporters apparently have different views. This is a problem that some leaders in some parties are up against from time to time.
I feel it is fair to say that while most hon. members who have spoken have said that they will vote for the bill, they have complained that it does not go far enough or that it goes too far in one direction or another. I should like, in closing this debate, to refer to some of the reservations or hesitations that have been voiced.
Several hon. members who have spoken have expressed the view that the financial needs of the universities will not be assisted by this bill, in fact if anything that the bill will aggravate their financial problems. I should point out, of course, this bill is not, ana was not intended to be, a comprehensive measure dealing with the whole university eaucational problem. Its purpose is very simple, to relieve the immediate financial problems of university students, making it financially possible, in other words, by way of loans, for any boy or girl with the necessary qualifications to contribute to his or her education in the post-secondary school level. It has been suggested that the federal government should do more to meet the financial problems of the universities. Let me make it quite clear that I agree that the universities need more, much more, in the way of financial assistance. However, whether it should come directly from the federal government or whether it should come from the provinces which, under our constitution, are responsible for education, is a question of opinion.
No, a question of the constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With the greatest respect, on the basis of what has been said in this debate over the last few days I suggest it is a question of opinion.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would go further and say this is not something we are likely to resolve in the course of this debate. In the meantime let me remind hon. members of what the federal government is doing at present for the universities, and I would like to make it perfectly clear that this is not a question of one party or another. What I am going to put on the record is, in the main, a list of programs introduced some time ago and endorsed, followed and adopted by both the principal parties in this country.
That does not make it right, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not for a moment suggesting that majority opinion makes anything right but, by the same token, I certainly do not agree that minority opinion makes anything right either.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The majority has some rights, even in this country.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The minister said that the amount that was paid out in connection with vocational training in the last fiscal year was one hundred and some million dollars. What fiscal year does he have reference to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The last fiscal year.
Well, what is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The last fiscal year?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, as my right hon. friend knows, the fiscal year ends in March.
Does the minister say those are the figures from March 1963 to March 1964?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the best of my knowledge.
You had better look them up again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am very happy at any time to have advice or help from the right hon.
Loans to Students
Leader of the Opposition, particularly in financial and economic matters, because I must say he has got a great head for figures. If the figure I am talking about applies to the current fiscal year instead of the last one I shall be glad to make the correction tomorrow.
It applies to the last year we were in office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I think I might be permitted to let that pass. Lately the right hon. gentleman has been doing a lot of reminiscing about the days he was in office. He made two speeches on the subject in the last 10 days, and I am sure we will hear more of them and will be interested in what he has to say.
All I ask is that you give the facts. Don't quote statistics that are not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I never thought the day would come when the right hon. gentleman would emphasize the need for giving the facts, but I am grateful to him for his remarks and perhaps we may hold him to them some day.
What about "Troubled Canada"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Read it again if you want to. I seem to have been diverted from what I was saying about the $265 million per annum which is being transferred from federal to provincial revenues. As I mentioned a few minutes ago, this is a very considerable sum of money and anyone who thinks about it and then suggests the present government is ignoring this extremely important and pressing problem, and suggests the federal government is doing nothing about it, is simply talking through his hat.
On their own, the universities have established a public commission under the very distinguished chairmanship of Dean Vincent Bladen of the University of Toronto, which soon will be holding meetings across Canada. This will help publicize the problems the universities are up against and I shall be surprised if, when it has finished its public hearings, it does not come up with recommendations as to how to deal best with these problems.
All of us know that in the years ahead we shall need more universities and far more university teachers. This is not a new problem. It has been known to everyone who has had an interest in universities and university education for nearly a decade and, if I may be permitted to say so, it was stressed in the

Loans to Students
report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects as far back as 1956. If hon. members will bear with me I should like to quote from what that commission had to say on this question in its first report of December 1956. I do so because of some of the things which have been said in the course of this debate. It says this:
If salary scales are increased substantially-
The report was talking about university teachers' salaries-
-and if the whole status of the university teaching profession in Canada is raised and improved, it should become increasingly easier to persuade young Canadians of high quality to enter the teaching profession. Furthermore, it should be possible for Canadian universities to attract to their ranks Canadians and others who are at present teaching in United States colleges and, in addition, a number of scientists and scholars from Europe and elsewhere. What is being suggested in essence is that a deliberate and sustained effort be made to raise the quality and standards of Canadian universities to among the highest prevailing anywhere in the world. It is perhaps not going too far to suggest that no other single course of action would be so likely to have such an important and fundamental effect upon the long term economic prospects for Canada.
In addition to the sums required for increased salaries, the existing universities and the new universities which will soon be needed will require substantial capital grants, if they are to take care of the very large increase in the anticipated enrolment. It is estimated that capital expenditures of about $1 billion will be required for these purposes over the period of the next 25 years.
It is of the greatest importance also that no Canadian boy or girl of ability should be denied a university education because he or she is unable to afford it. University costs are quite obviously going to increase considerably, and it would seem reasonable to expect that some part of this increase should be recovered through an increase in student fees. This should not be done, however, unless adequate provision is made through a combination of scholarships, bursaries and student loan funds to take care of those students who require financial assistance.
It is not the responsibility of this commission to recommend how the financial problems of the universities should be solved. It is our duty however, to point out most emphatically that it is vitally important to Canada's future for the status of our universities to be improved and strengthened and for their facilities to be increased.
As the author of those words-and I wrote them myself, if I remember correctly-may I say I think they are as true today as when they were written nearly eight years ago.
Where are the bursaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not believe enough has been done to meet the problem which now confronts our universities. The result is that some qualified and deserving students could be denied a university education in Canada

because facilities are insufficient and I am sure all hon. members would agree with me that this would be a shame.
It is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While I am expressing some personal opinions may I add that despite what the royal commission had to say in 1956 about student fees, in my view, in my personal view, education at university level, like primary and secondary education, should be free for everyone who has the necessary qualifications.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I see my good friend the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) applauding and I hope he will not call me a pseudoLiberal again.
All you have to do is put it into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there are to be fees, there should be scholarships and bursaries to meet them.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Bring on the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not expect this will happen overnight but I do believe it will come to pass, and I hope it will come to pass very soon.
This having been said, perhaps we should remind ourselves that what we are doing now is to consider legislation which is before us dealing with one aspect of this problem only, that is authorizing the banks to make loans to students under certain specified conditions.
I should like to turn to another subject which was raised first, I think, during the course of the debate by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and then by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). This was the question whether the amount of $40 million per annum plus an appropriate increase based on the increase in the 18-24 year age group would be sufficient to take care of all the applications for student loans which may be expected. Perhaps I did not give a sufficiently clear or comprehensive answer at the time to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and I should like to go into this now in a little more detail.
The estimates I am about to put on record, now, were arrived at after consultation with provincial and university authorities who have experience in these matters. First, in the academic year 1964, there will be about
221,000	students in universities, teachers col-

leges and vocational training institutions. It is estimated that one out of three of these students, that is, about 74,000, will receive loans which, according to estimates made by those who have been engaged in this field, would possibly average about $500. If these estimates are correct, this would amount to something less than $40 million and my advice is that these estimates are probably somewhat on the high side. It would be appreciated that these 74,000 students would include those in their first, second, third and fourth years of undergraduate work in addition to those carrying out graduate studies. It is assumed, that the university population will increase at about the rate of 10 per cent per annum. If this proves to be accurate then in the second year there should be around 81,000 students requiring loans. Those in their fourth year of undergraduate work will have graduated, but they will be replaced by students entering university for the first time. This means that an additional $40 million will be required for this purpose a year from now-
Does the hon. gentleman mean $40 million of additional money in the next academic year plus the money necessary to pay loans to students who are taking their second year at university?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I mean that according to these calculations, a year from now about
81,000	students will need assistance in this way. I should make it clear that this is on a national basis including the province of Quebec which I intend to deal with later. The increase from 74,000 this year to 81,000 next year means that a year from now another $40 million will be needed in addition to the $40 million which will be provided this year. A second $40 million will be provided plus an amount to take care of the increase in the age group 18-24.
Is the minister suggesting that 80,000 students will be covered by $40 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
At an average of $500 apiece?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
They are not going to be very generous loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, these estimates were prepared by people who have had a good many years of experience in
Loans to Students
this field. They felt that only about one in three of the students would need this kind of help or would want it, and they felt that on the average the loans would not amount to $1,000, which is the limit in any one year, but to an average of about $500. If we find that this is too little, then I will certainly have no hesitation, despite the length of the present debate, in coming back to the house for an increase in the provision. I must say, though, Mr. Speaker, that the people whom we have consulted in this field think that, if anything, the amounts we have provided will not be used up to the full. I must take their advice, because they are the best people, with the best experience, that we have been able to find.
I want to go on with these calculations to make sure that all hon. members at least know the basis upon which they are made. There would be some repayments commencing some 18 months or two years from now, but these would be relatively negligible to start with. However, they would tend to reduce to some extent the amount outstanding. Such reductions would be offset by the steady increase in the university population each year and the corresponding increase in the total amount required for loan purposes each year over and above the original amount of $40 million per annum. Taking everything into account, it is estimated that the total amount outstanding will increase at the rate of about $40 million plus per annum over the first five-year period. It is therefore estimated that some $200 million to perhaps $250 million might be outstanding five years from now. From then on the rate of increase might be expected to be somewhat higher as the total population in the university age group grows. Having reviewed these calculations once again over the week end in the light of the comments made by the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), I think they are probably as reasonable as it is possible to be until we have had some experience in this field ourselves.
I would like to turn to another series of questions, Mr. Speaker. A number of hon. members have criticized the bill on constitutional or legal grounds. I am grateful to them for their comments, and I am especially grateful to my friend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for the way in which he put his views before the house. The hon. member is a senior and respected member of the bar of Ontario who has had wide

Loans to Students
experience in matters of this kind, and his opinions not only deserve to be taken seriously, but I can assure him, Mr. Speaker, that they have been taken seriously by the government.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Taken seriously, but thrown out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I was just going to say that I am also very grateful to my parliamentary secretary, not only for the searching examination he has made, with the responsible officers of the Department of Justice, of the various points that have been raised, but also, if I may say so, for the very able and, to me, very convincing way in which he explained the government's position in the house.
Hear, hear.
You never said that about me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) said I never said that about him; but the fact is that he never gave a legal opinion in the house, and I hope he does not start now. The hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Pennell) is also a distinguished member of the Ontario bar. I think I am particularly fortunate in having him to assist me. Not only is he able and industrious, but I am sure all hon. members *envy him his honeyed tongue.
I am not a lawyer and I can only offer a layman's opinion of the three points that have been raised. First of all, my parliamentary secretary has stated that the government would accept a change along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). As I understand it, this is a matter of drafting. I think the draftsmen feel quite confident that the present wording would cover the point raised by the hon. member for Yukon. However, I would not like there to be any doubts in his mind on this score, so when we reach that point at the committee stage, we will introduce an amendment which I think-which I hope; I should not say "I think"-will satisfy him.
I have no difficulty, as I have indicated, with the point raised by the hon. member for Greenwood. After very serious and careful consideration, I am advised that in the opinion of the law officers, and also of hon. members who are members of the legal profession, this proposal is unnecessary.
The third point that has been raised in this general area deals with the question of lend-

ing money to minors. I certainly shall not attempt to discuss the legal arguments that have been raised; but I would like to make two points. The first is that the bill is intended to provide loans to students to assist them with their university education or their vocational training. If money is to be lent to them rather than given to them in one way or another, there must be some provision to ensure that it is paid back. There are good precedents for this, as the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand explained the other night. As I understand it, it is a matter of banking law. This is the point that some hon. members today, and perhaps last week, have failed to deal with. I, as a layman, am prepared to agree that there is room for differences on many legal questions. Perhaps if there were not, we would not need so many lawyers. But the fact is that there is room for differences of opinion. I appreciate the opinions that have been offered by members of opposition parties, but I am sure they will not take offence if, after much additional discussion and consideration, I have decided to accept the advice and opinions of those whose job it is to advise the government in these matters.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Even if they are wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I was just going to say that if their advice is wrong there will be an opportunity, no doubt, for the courts to rule upon it; and after all, this will keep a lot of very-
Careful. You are going to say something you should not say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it will keep a lot of people busy; I will leave it at that. In the meantime I hope we shall be able to get on with the business of making loans to students. Personally I am completely confident that practically all these loans will be repaid. We have heard a lot in this house today about protests from students in regard to this legislation; but believe me, Mr. Speaker, there are a whole lot of students right across the country who want to see this measure passed.
A lot of students would like to have it passed, but not with this principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The second point I wish to make in this connection is that some hon. members of certain opposition parties-not all -have argued that in some way the constitution is being trampled on and the rights of the provinces affronted. I must say that I find this line of argument quite uncon-

vincing and I will give my reasons. In the first place, officials of all provincial governments met with federal officials to discuss the form of the legislation, and as I said in answer to a question today I should like to acknowledge the very real assistance which those provincial officials gave to us in the formulation and drafting of this plan. I am assured that they found the bill quite satisfactory as far as they were concerned. I have the privilege of knowing some of these officials, and believe me they are just as jealous of the rights of the provinces as are a lot of other people. I might add that this matter was discussed at the last federal-provincial conference, and it was stated then with no equivocation that if any province felt it had a perfectly good scheme which was working well and did not wish to participate in this particular scheme, then that was all right as far as the federal government was concerned. As hon. members know there is a provision in the bill which provides that if any of the provinces wish to carry on with their own schemes and do not wish to participate in the federal scheme they should notify the federal government within 30 days, I think it is, of the passing of the act that they plan to continue their own scheme. In such case such provinces will receive compensation equal to the net cost to the federal government which would be incurred if the scheme had applied to such province.
As I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, the prime minister of Quebec has advised me that in the case of the province of Quebec that province will continue with its present scheme and take advantage of clause 12 of the bill, I think it is. I suppose that because I come from Ontario the hon. member for Lapointe might think I do not fully understand matters in Quebec. I certainly did not intend to be sharp or offhand with him during the question period today, but it has always been my understanding that the prime minister of Quebec was in a position to speak for the government of Quebec and for the very considerable majority of the people of Quebec. Until I am convinced to the contrary I think that is good enough for me.
Is the minister suggesting that members from the various provinces cannot speak for their own province as well, that they are subjugated or relegated behind the provincial premier?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not only did I not suggest or think that for one moment, but I think all hon. members, particularly those from the
Loans to Students
province of Quebec in the party to which my hon. friend belongs, have made it very clear that they are quite competent to express views on this very important subject at some considerable length. While I am on this point -and I did not mean to bring this up-may I say I was interested to see that the leader of the Conservative party from Quebec had one point of view, which I thought he expressed very well, but that his followers do not apparently go along with him. However, that is their privilege.
We have seen that in your own house too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member is talking about my house or my party. If he is talking about my house I do not know that I should engage in a personal discussion of that kind. These things happen in the best of families where there are differences of view, and I expect they always will.

May I put a question to the minister on that subject. Did he receive any communication from the president of the students association of Quebec in the province of Quebec, and did the minister agree to meet representatives of the students tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To be perfectly honest, I do not know. I left here at six o'clock; I did not get to my office till about a quarter to seven. I made it clear to my secretary earlier in the day that if anyone wanted to see me at any time I should be more than delighted to see them; and if this included the students from the province of Quebec they would be doubly welcome. I would be delighted to have the opportunity to explain to them not only the provisions of this bill and what it will mean to the students all over the country, but also the reasons why in their province their government has found it unnecessary to go along with this plan.
I think I have only one other point I wish to mention, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam questioned me about why under this bill the lending of money was restricted to the banks, and about whether or not it should be extended to include the credit unions and the caisse populaires. I should point out what our experience has been under other guaranteed loan arrangements. I think it is only the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which recognizes credit unions as lenders, together with the chartered banks. The other acts, the Farm Improvement

Division
Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act, recognize the banks only.
The reasons for including credit unions under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act were, first, that the credit unions wished to be included, and second, because of the relative importance of credit unions in the fisheries industry in regions where service by the chartered banks is limited. The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act came into force in 1955 and a total of $1,900,000 has been lent by all lenders from its inception up to March 31, 1964. Actual lending by the credit unions under the act has been negligible; loans made by credit unions have amounted to only 6 per cent of the total. Only three credit unions made loans under the act. One of these credit unions made one loan and another made five loans. A total of 59 loans was made by all credit unions in an amount of $117,470, all on the west coast. Perhaps I should also add that no loans have been made by any credit union since 1961. In these circumstances there did not seem to be a great deal of point in expanding this beyond the chartered banks. I have tried to answer some of the more important questions that have been raised and I will be glad to discuss the clauses when we are in committee.
I declare the motion carried.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Short title.

Mr. Chairman, on October 4, 1957, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics put a rocket into propulsion, Sputnik No. 1. A sophisticated mechanism put together by mathematics, physics, astronomy, chemistry and biology shocked the western world and brought to our attention that the universities have much to give to the development of

our society. This one event, more than any other in the last decade, has focused the attention of the western world on the problems of education. We suddenly realized that Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton-universities like McGill, Queen's, Montreal, British Columbia and Toronto have great things to give in the struggles of the west.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I bring to the attention of hon. members of the committee that it is a bit noisy and very difficult for the Chair to follow the interesting remarks of the hon. member.

I thank you, Mr. Chairman. In discussing the problems of training the young people of Canada we should look at certain important statistics. One half of the population is under 25 years of age; about 7.9 per cent is over 65; one half of the population is supporting the other half. According to present trends, by 1971 the percentage of persons in the 30 to 40 age group will have shrunk. Mr. Bascom St. John in a recent article in the Globe and Mail reported that the American council on education had shown there were 5 million unemployed but that 4 million job opportunities were not filled.
It is projected that within six years half the available population will be in technical and highly skilled occupations. The demand for unskilled workers will decrease and the demand for semi-professional and technical personnel will increase by 40 per cent, and for clerical sales employment by 26 per cent. Our society faces a most important social and economic revolution, being brought on through the processes of automation. Our system of production and distribution is being radically transformed.
There are three basic elements in automation: (1) controls like the simple thermostat in your home, which represent the selfregulating system and can make men superfluous; (2) the electronic computer which can add electric impulses and stores information. It has a capacity to perform logical decision making. The third unique factor in the automated economy is the automation assembly line.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but it is my duty to remind him that even though wide latitude is allowed on the first clause of the bill I do not think he can go on discussing education in general. I suggest to him that his remarks should be more precisely directed to the question of loans for students, which is the matter now
Loans to Students
before the committee. I would like him to bear that in mind in continuing his remarks.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I am drawing a picture to show the need for highly trained, technical personnel and the importance of the universities in providing these personnel. The system of helping people to go to universities to get this training is very important.
I maintain we shall have to devote to education a larger proportion of our economic resources. We must take stock of what we are doing and consider the training which is to be given, in the light of the shortage of highly skilled workers in this country. We have spent a great deal of time in this house discussing the control of our industry. If we do not produce highly qualified people who are capable of managing our industry, but have to import them from other countries, this, too, will be a result of how we handle our affairs in the field of education. I believe the whole context of these discussions must be kept in mind when we are talking about financing a generation of Canadians so that they can be trained to fill this great need.
We are in danger of finding ourselves with a class of the functionally illiterate whose poverty is not hereditary because it is congenital, but hereditary due to social and economic factors. Our present system is likely to produce a class of poverty stricken people whose inheritance does not give them the chance to drag themselves out of their depressed state. I believe this bill is one more facet of a program which will help our people to improve the faculties which will fit them for the highly sophisticated economic society which we are developing.
In the over-all training of Canadians we are not doing a great deal. The government of Canada is carrying on joint programs with the provinces but the number of people involved in these programs is very small and the majority of these are in technical secondary schools. Again, more than half of the students in such schools are studying office routine, bookkeeping, and so on. The number engaged in technical training to meet the great and growing demands of our society for specialized skills is really very small.
Another problem is presented by school drop-outs. About one third of those entering elementary schools drop out before they reach grade eight. Another one third drop out before they have completed high school. The number of people who enter our educational system and who reap the full advan-

Loans to Students
tage of the opportunity provided for them is very few. I believe we must use the means we are discussing this evening, and further means, as well, to ensure that people who enter our educational system will emerge trained and able to take their places in society. A study was recently made by the Department of Labour showing the number of vacancies existing in Canada in the highly trained professions. It was found there were 32,785 in engineering; 14,516 in natural sciences and 1,841 in social sciences. The projected vacancies by 1967 show that positions available in engineering are likely to increase by 32 percent, in natural sciences by 31 per cent, and in the social sciences by 88 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is with great hesitation that I again call upon the hon. member who has the floor to limit his remarks to the question before the committee, which is the question of loans to students.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I feel that the urgent requirements of Canadian society and of the Canadian economy demand that both at the federal level of government and at the provincial level we should mobilize our resources toward the establishment of the most effective possible education program, and this bill now before us is one more means to assist students to enter universities and equip themselves for the many important tasks which face us as a nation in this day and age.
We must view the problem of education today as something which cannot be divorced from the development of our society in general. There are many revolutionary factors at work changing the economy and changing the social life of Canada in 1964. We need measures such as have been brought before us this evening, so as to enable our students to equip themselves to cope with these changes and take their places in the economic and social life of this country, not forgetting the point made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), that it should be an education with a high moral purpose so that the direction of this country may be in democratic and liberal hands to give leadership toward the goals we all desire.

Mr. Chairman, if I rise again in this debate, it is not in order to resort to some "dirty and nasty" tactics, as some hon. members said this afternoon, but, on the contrary to follow up the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who stated in his speech that those who were opposed to this

legislation had advanced some arguments which did not convince him, or rather, which failed to make him understand our opposition to this bill.
May I say to the minister that listening to his remarks, I became more and more convinced that I should oppose the bill, because the arguments he himself advanced were wrong. He based his thesis on three main points:
First of all, with regard to the constitutional character of the legislation, his main argument was that provincial officials co-operated in the preparation of this bill.
That is a new constitutional theory. There is no more need of a supreme court, a higher court or a court of appeal, according to the Minister of Finance, as the officials representing the various provinces can just meet to study a bill. In that case, the advice or opinions they express, the decisions they take, become law and can turn anything unconstitutional into something fully constitutional. That was the most important argument of the Minister of Finance.
As his second argument, the minister said: This legislation is constitutional, because there is a section providing for replacement payments; there is a formula of compensation or option and therefore, this legislation is constitutional. Another very strong argument.
And the third argument is the ex cathedra argument, striking and overwhelmingly; Premier Lesage approved this legislation.
Because of a premier's opinion, we should once again proclaim as being constitutional something which is not constitutional. Besides, it is not surprising to see Hon. Jean Lesage support such a theory of co-operative federalism, because he himself bears the responsibility of having been in 1958 the legislator of the Liberal party program to assist universities.
But the minister's arguments cannot modify in the least the point of view that I had an opportunity to put forward during the debate on second reading of this bill; it cannot be changed either by the arguments put forward by the supporters of centralization. My hon. friends opposite, representing the province of Quebec, have once again voted in a way which does not tally with the fine theories of the last election campaigns. We, Quebec Conservatives, have voted in accordance with the policies we had indicated.
The supporters of this interference of the federal government in the field of education, under this legislation, take their stand on five main arguments.

In the first place, the ancillary theory, according to which the federal government, having exclusive jurisdiction on matters and subjects listed in section 91, is interfering in a field which is related to the main object which is at the basis of the legislation.
It is by virtue of this ancillary theory that we have the federal authority in matters of education and schooling among Indians, since the Indian problem comes under the federal government. So the privy council gave two main and necessary reasons for the application of the ancillary theory; but such is not the case in the consideration of the present legislation.
First of all as I said a while ago, the subject of the legislation should come exclusively under federal jurisdiction. Second, the privy council decided that it was necessary that this legislation be required.
I do not see, in the consideration of this legislation providing for the making of loans to students, that we are in a field coming, first of all, exclusively under the provisions of section 91.
Consequently, ancillary power cannot be put forward in this legislation, for, by virtue section 93, the provincial government alone has jurisdiction in matters of education.
We see the supporters of co-operative federalism, which is a centralizing measure in disguise, propound other arguments in favour of the adoption of this legislation. The main one is the financial inability of the provinces, or else, the urgency of the problem.
I do not feel that the Minister of Finance can seriously raise the argument of the needs of the provinces to justify the introduction of this legislation.
I beg the Minister of Finance to stop correcting his text for ten seconds at the most, and I shall venture to suggest some means to him for making this legislation constitutional.
Why should not the provinces instead of the banks, be the lending institutions?
Should the federal government allow the provinces, instead of the banks, to make loans to their students, the provinces, which are well aware of the educational needs of their population and have sole jurisdiction, by virtue of the constitution, to issue studies and capacity certificates, could, in turn, make interest free loans to students.
The law would be the same; the aim of this government would be the same; the result would be as efficient and the Canadian constitution would be respected.
Loans to Students
Why lend through banks? Why beat around the bush, when there is a very simple means?
