Let the government amend its legislation so that the provinces will be the lending agencies instead of the banks; then the federal government will pay, apart from the taxes and revenues of the provinces, an amount of money which might be used according to the principles mentioned in this bill. Then nobody will be able to question the legality or constitutionality of this legislation. But no. Federal legislation in the field of education goes back to 1913, when the first legislation was imposed and adopted by the federal government following a recommendation by the royal commission on industrial and technical education.
If we read the conclusions of this report, on pages 11 and 12 of volume 1, we see the following recommendation:
Considering what the teaching of those various branches in primary schools will cost and remembering that such a school work was not considered as within the field of public education, at the time of confederation, when the provinces accepted the responsibility for legislation to maintain and control education within their boundaries, the commission recommends the setting up of a fund intended to subsidise provincial governments during a period of 10 years.
Subsequently a bill which authorized a subsidy of $350,000 per year to the provinces for a period of 10 years was passed. Although it was a rather high amount at the time, it was nevertheless the first intrusion by the federal government in the field of education.
And that is not all. At that time the promoters of centralization or federalism were proud of this result and said that a commission had just proclaimed a national need or necessity in order to justify a subsidy system.
Today, there are three theses by which it is endeavoured to explain and justify the intrusion of the federal government in the field of education.
First, there was that theory under which this ancillary power referred to previously can be connected with execution of one of the powers explicitly mentioned in section 91.
Second, this educational theory is explained by the activities of federal organizations such as the C.B.C. and the national film board.
And the third system is that of grants which, in 1913, resulted in the first intrusion of the federal government in the field of education. That intrusion was followed in 1940 by that of the Rowell-Sirois commission. At that time this commission recognized definitely the exclusive jurisdiction of

Loans to Students
the provinces in the field of education. Referring to certain conclusions of the report, we find that:
The instruction of the young during their formative years is a matter which the provinces must continue to control. A free hand in something so important to the social and cultural life of the people seems to us to be vital to any provincial autonomy worthy of the name, and it is obvious that any attempt to alter the existing arrangements would meet with powerful opposition and would provoke profound resentment.
Even at that time, the theory concerning federal grants to universities was taking form. It was in 1955 or 1956 that another commission, the Massey-Levesque commission, introduced the educational system which today enables our hon. friends opposite to bring forward this measure, under the pretext that it is along the same line of thought as the legislation passed to come to the aid of universities, and which came as a result of a recommendation of the Massey-Levesque commission, that is that the federal government should enter the field of education through grants to universities.
During the debate on second reading of the bill, we heard several members opposite suggest or point out that the measure brought forward by the Minister of Finance was similar in nature to the one introduced by the Conservative government, under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition. I submit that this is false, because when the Conservative government came into office, there was a crucial problem which brought the Quebec government and the federal government into conflict. At that time grants to universities were frozen, because the universities themselves were aware that education could not come under federal jurisdiction, except in extraordinary cases such as minorities provided in section 93.
Afterwards there was the Barrette, Sauve, Diefenbaker formula which allowed the adoption of a measure granting the province of Quebec a 1 per cent abatement while respecting the Canadian constitution. At that time, the Conservative government did not introduce centralizing legislation, because Mr. Fleming, the then minister of finance-and in that connection I quoted part of his comments when I spoke last Wednesday-stated that it was a temporary solution and that the Conservatives should correct a centralization advocated by the Liberals, as they are now doing.
Mr. Chairman, under the pretext of referring to this precedent, to the effect that the Conservatives have found a solution to this

constitutional problem, here is an attempt being made today to make us believe that the piece of legislation submitted by the present Minister of Finance is constitutional, because some officials have approved it; in the second place, because there are compensation payments; third, because the premier, Mr. Jean Lesage, seems to approve it.
I respectfully suggest that this argument does not change in any way the fundamentals, and I cannot understand, really, how it is that Liberal members from the province of Quebec-whether they are ministers or private members-in all conscientiousness, rose a few minutes ago and forgot that the autonomy of the province of Quebec is a vital question.
As long as public men who represent the interests of that province will fail to do their duty, we shall constantly have to face the centralization crisis now prevailing in the province of Quebec.
That is true.

Another theory designed to explain the interference of the federal government in the field of education is due to the report of the Massey-Levesque commission, because a distinction was at that time made between education and culture.
I have here a few notes on this subject; unfortunately, I do not wish to delay unduly the passage of this bill.
Oh, oh.

I actually said "the passage of this bill". I see that those members from Quebec are anxious to pass this bill as soon as possible. They seem annoyed when we speak about the bill.
I wonder how the hon. member for Lon-gueuil (Mr. C6te) during the next election campaign, will defend the centralizing attitude he advocates tonight through his failure to understand? He does not understand that the present government-the government he supports, the political party he belongs to- advocates a unitary system instead of respecting the federalism of the Canadian constitution. There again, under the pretext that it is required by the common good, attempts will be made to justify the legislation being introduced.
But then, the Canadian constitution, the Quebec resolutions and the London resolutions do not even mention education and do not make any distinction between culture and education gained outside school; neither is there any mention of the new centralizing theory advocated by our friends opposite.

I cannot understand why some members are today adhering to such a harmful theory, because beyond federalism of the Canadian constitution, which is composed of 10 provinces, there is a federalism of cultures, of nations, that is the cultures of the French-Canadian and the English nations.
As long as we do not understand and respect this confederation, this federalism of Canadian cultures, we will not be able to achieve the true general unity for which all members have legitimate aspirations. Unfortunately, because of political interests, they do not have the courage to respect the Canadian constitution, to rise and vote against their own government when the Quebec autonomy is at stake.
Another reason why centralizing people are in favour of the theory advocated by the government and the Minister of Finance is the common good principle, which brings about a Unitarian system instead of complete respect of the Canadian constitution.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to add to what I had already said. I hope that clause 1 of the bill will allow the great jurists, my hon. friends from Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) and from Levis (Mr. Guay), as well as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets), who are learned jurists, as I said, to refute the legal argument I have put forward tonight concerning the respect of the Canadian constitution.
But I fear that they remain seated according to the line of least resistance. Moreover, it is rather embarrassing to speak against one's convictions; but it is even more embarrassing to depend entirely upon a political party rather than upon one's fellow countrymen and fellow citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I shall have other suggestions to make in due course, when we look into the various clauses of this bill; I hope that the Minister of Finance will, for the time being, consider the possibility of amending this legislation so that the federal government gives up to the provinces more of their direct taxation fields or that the Minister of Finance convinces his cabinet colleagues to appoint the provinces as lending institutions instead of the banks.
Then there will be no doubt that the federal government, under this legislation, strives to respect our Canadian constitution and, according to our common hope, help the students in the whole of Canada, while respecting fully and completely the British North America Act.
Loans to Students
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member suggested that the provinces be appointed as lending institutions. Would he favour the idea of the provinces getting credit from the Bank of Canada, instead of levying heavier taxes on the taxpayers?
Mr. Chairman, I think that my hon. friend would be better advised to call on the hon. members opposite who, some time ago, advocated the debt free money policy.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak a second time on Bill No. C-110, an act to facilitate the making of loans to students.
There is one sure thing, it is that in the last few days, in spite of the wish of all hon. members to hurry as much as possible the business of the house, that bill has prompted several hon. members to make a speech, enabled journalists to write several articles and some citizens to protest against its passing, in addition to allowing the students of the province of Quebec to prove that they are serious when they talk about respecting the rights of the provinces within confederation.
Mr. Chairman, I was surprised a little earlier to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) enumerate the fields of activity in which the federal government has co-operated in the last few years.
The minister spoke of the field of education and I was astonished to hear him speak with pride of the various steps taken by the federal government to assist education in Canada.
He mentioned the $2 per capita grants to university students and the income tax abatement equivalent to $2 per capita which was granted to Quebec. He referred to the scholarships awarded by the national research council and those given by the atomic energy control board which total approximately $1,250,000. He also spoke of the Canada council grants to universities and students. He mentioned the loans for the construction of student residences and the grants for technical and professional training. He also mentioned the sums of money the federal government had paid out to the provinces in the form of taxes. In any case, the amount was one of $500 million, if you add the figures mentioned by the Minister of Finance, an amount which would be paid by the federal government to the provinces or directly to the universities and students, in the field of education.
5732

Loans to Students
If we examine this list, it is easy to see that the door is now wide open. They started by opening it slowly, but now it is wide open. Not only is Ottawa making itself at home, but, as the Minister of Finance pointed out a few moments ago, it feels proud to be able to prove that the federal government has directly intruded upon the field of education. It is more than a stealthy entrance, it is now direct. Indeed, it is being officially announced, and the Minister of Finance is quoting figures and explaining what the federal government intends to do in the field of education.
But what surprised me most was how much the Minister of Finance seems happy and satisfied to be able to say: The premier of Quebec does not protest, the premier of Quebec seems to agree, the premier of Quebec approves of the legislation.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the Minister of Finance has begun to judge his man; he has begun to know the premier of Quebec. He has already seen Mr. Lesage come to Ottawa and, a few days before the general election of last April 8, state in no uncertain terms: We need 25 per cent of individual income taxes, 25 per cent of corporation income taxes and 100 per cent of succession duties. That was an ultimatum.
But the federal Minister of Finance succeeded in getting on the right side of the premier of Quebec because the latter had withdrawn his words. He retracted and he accepted the few crumbs the Minister of Finance offered him in return.
Fortified by that success, by the knowledge he had of the premier of Quebec, aware that the present premier of Quebec talks a lot but does very little-that is nothing at all-spends a lot but doesn't think much-I am speaking of the premier of Quebec-the Minister of Finance succeeded once again the same feat of strength by letting the premier of Quebec yap, then gradually silencing him and taming him like a gentle little lamb.
In fact, we remember that the day after the last federal-provincial conference Premier Lesage said: "If the federal government introduces its bill concerning loans to students, if it does anything whatsoever in the field of education, we will sue it."
The first time, it was an ultimatum: "Do it, or else... This was serious. It was the first time that a premier from the province of Quebec dared rise and speak his mind to the authorities in Ottawa. But Mr. Lesage gave ground that time.
[Mr. Grfgoire.l
Now, for the second time, he is backing down, unless he is perhaps holidaying somewhere, or is not aware of what is going on in Ottawa, ignorant of the fact that at present, the federal government is interfering more directly and more deeply in the educational field. So much so that he remains speechless, silent as the grave. He has given way a second time.
The Minister of Finance can rejoice. He has not succeeded in silencing the premier of the province of Quebec but he will let the crisis pass, aware of the fact that, later on, the Quebec premier will be again as gentle as a lamb.
However, the Minister of Finance should not think that because Premier Lesage says nothing the province of Quebec is in favour of the new legislation. Far from it.
The Quebec premier talks a lot but he seldom acts accordingly. He made fine pledges. He promised free education; in fact, that was a plank in his 1960 and 1962 platforms but he never carried out that promise. We never had free education and we are going to wait a long while before we get it.

subtopic: CONFINEMENT OF JUVENILES IN FEDERAL PENITENTIARIES
CONFINEMENT OF JUVENILES IN FEDERAL PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 15 last, I asked the Minister of Justice what steps were going to be taken by the government to implement the report of the commission on juvenile delinquency. I have put three questions on the order paper with regard to this matter. I asked a question on June 18 to which the Minister of Justice graciously replied that we would look into the matter. On July 15 the Speaker considered this question should once again be put on the order paper.
My submission briefly is this, that in the last ten years we are putting twice as many children in the penitentiary-when I am talking about the penitentiary, I mean the penitentiary for adults-than we were before. I say immediately our treatment of those we classify as juvenile delinquents must be immediately overhauled. Since my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, I am going to take the liberty of reading this statement.
I have pressed reform on many occasions in the House of Commons, and in particular I spoke with regard to the matter in 1961, as recorded on page 5351 of Hansard for that date, and again on May 31, 1963 as recorded at page 518 of Hansard. It is shocking to learn and appreciate that children are still being incarcerated in the penitentiary. This fact is now confirmed by a committee on juvenile delinquency organized by the Department of Justice and chosen from their personnel. The personnel of the committee are, the commissioner of penitentiaries, Mr. Allen J. MacLeod, who heads the committee on juvenile delinquency-who says frankly that he is worried-Dr. L. P. Gendreau, penitentiary service psychiatrist; Inspector E. W. Willes, R.C.M.P., Ronald R. Price, a justice department lawyer and Miss J. L. Lynch, a member of the national parole board.
The committee on juvenile delinquency went across the country and examined the various situations in the various penitentiaries. It was organized and set up for the purpose of ascertaining the facts with regard to Canadian children incarcerated in Canadian penitentiaries, which means they are held in custody for more than a two-year term. The man behind the investigation was Allen J. MacLeod, one of the commissioners of the penitentiaries, and a very fine article was written on this subject by Bill Trent, Weekend Magazine staff writer. One of the reformers said:

I was a juvenile delinquent myself. I was the leader of a small gang. And if it hadn't been for the cop on the beat-a wonderful guy who took an interest in us all-God knows where I'd be today.
My answer to that question is that he might have been in the penitentiary along with many young girls and boys. It is interesting to look at the facts. In 1952, there were 4,700 prisoners incarcerated in Canadian penitentiaries, and by 1962 there were 7,100 living under crowded and unusual conditions. The largest increase was amongst youngsters of 16 years and under. There were 32 admitted in 1952 and 84 in 1962. There are 1,091 inmates under 21 years now in our penitentiaries and one is 14 years of age.
The committee discovered some strange facts. Not so long ago a 12-year old boy found himself in the St. Vincent de Paul federal training centre, and everyone in the women's Kingston penitentiary recalls a tiny 14-year old girl who went behind the walls to serve a two year term for stealing a bicycle. In Dorchester penitentiary in New Brunswick, one of the boys was so small the guards were afraid he might squeeze out between the bars. I took the time to check up on this article that Trent wrote with one of the commissioners of the penitentiary and I found that these are facts. In 1962, we put three times as many children in jail as we did in 1952, and the trend continues. This was the reason the then minister of justice set up the committee.
This is a shocking thing. I see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice is here this evening. It is a shocking thing for the people of Canada to learn that section 12 of the Criminal Code states:
No person shall be convicted of an olfence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was under the age of seven years.
Provided a child of seven is sane and appreciates the nature and quality of his act, he can then be brought before a court, par-, ticularly in those provinces where the juvenile delinquents act does not apply, and be placed in a penitentiary with hardened criminals.
The definition of a crime is an act or omission prohibited under the penalty of the supreme power of the state, and any crime which calls for a penalty of more than two years under our Criminal Code, means the judge or magistrate may incarcerate a child, seven years or over, in a penitentiary-and they have been doing this very thing.
The only stipulation is that the child must be competent to know the nature and con-

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion sequence of his conduct and appreciate that his conduct is wrong. In 1959, there were 11,686 youngsters between seven and 15 years of age adjudged delinquent in Canada. Nineteen were seven years old. Ninety eight were eight years old.
One of the saddest stories is about an imprisoned 12 year old Quebec boy, who still remains anonymous, but who has gone down in penitentiary history as a classic case. He had all the cards stacked against him. He was the product of a shiftless father and a prostitute mother. One night he found his mother sleeping with the landlord. Furiously he picked up a can of tomatoes and hurled it at the man, striking him on the head. He was charged with assault. The judge, after considering the boy's record, sentenced him to two years in St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. He was placed there among hundreds of hardened criminals. Later he was transferred to a federal training centre because the warden "choked up". The boy was found to be polite and co-operative and responded to sympathy. The guards chipped in and bought him a scooter, a toy construction set and a fleet of trucks. He was refused the right to play outside.
No one will deny we have not come a long way in reform, but it is not enough. The committee found 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the potential juvenile delinquents can be recognized in school, but teachers have nowhere to turn. I believe the term "juvenile delinquent" should be dropped. It means too many things. It means anything from riding a bicycle on a sidewalk to committing one of the most heinous crimes in the code.
The question is, are we going to amend the code? Second, are we going to set up institutions where these young boys and girls can be educated and given the love and care they need, but which has been denied them because of their parents? Above all, are they going to be placed in institutions where they can be rehabilitated?
I have two points I wish to make, Mr. Speaker. I say that section 12 of the Criminal Code should be amended immediately. No child of seven years of age should be convicted in the same manner as a mature man or woman. That age should be raised to 13 years.
My second point is that children who do find themselves in difficulties should be placed in a rehabilitation home where they can be

educated and rehabilitated. When a child is born he is as pure as a white sheet of paper. It is the environment in which he finds himself that causes the trouble. What happens to him is due to many environmental factors, and mostly parents.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONFINEMENT OF JUVENILES IN FEDERAL PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any member of the house who will take issue with what the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) has said. The importance of the problem has been recognized both by the previous government and this one. The previous government established an expert committee to study juvenile delinquency and when the final report of the committee is received, which it is expected will be towards the end of this year, and its recommendations are made known with regard to the treatment of juvenile delinquency, all expedient action will be taken by this government to carry them into effect.
I would remind the house that already a substantial amount of work has been done towards establishing the kind of institution where training can be provided for young people under circumstances which should give them some opportunity of rehabilitating themselves in society, and when I say "institution" I do not mean the maximum security institution we commonly regard as covered by the term penitentiary.
Construction has already commenced on one of these institutions designed primarily for young offenders, at Cowansville, Quebec. Tenders will be called shortly for a second one at Springhill, Nova Scotia and in a matter of several months, possibly weeks, for a third at Warkworth, Ontario and-and I know this will be close to the heart of the hon. member-for a fourth at Drumheller, Alberta. I do not pretend that the establishment of institutions alone will achieve this particular end. We shall be relying on the committee to recommend changes in criminal procedure to take care of these young people. I shall be pleased to draw the attention of members of the committee to the recommendations the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) has made this evening, so that they may take them into consideration before making their final report.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.43 p.m.
